Article Title: Scientists examined 13 insects trapped in 99-million-year-old amber and identified a new species whose flexible mouthpart reached nearly twice its body length, possibly letting it probe deep into tree
Article Text:
Unique mouthparts that no longer exist

The forests and insects of the time

Not much in the world has survived to be known as old as the dinosaurs, but when it comes to a recently discovered insect species, the statement holds true. Some 99 million years ago, a tiny insect belonging to a previously unknown species became trapped in tree resin. The resin hardened and turned into amber; the fossil preserved within it has now led a team of researchers from the School of Zoology and The Steinhardt Museum of Natural History to identify and describe a new species named Cretodorus noonoo, or 'Noo-Noo'.The researchers examined insect fossils belonging to Neazoniidae, an ancient family of planthoppers, including 13 specimens preserved in Kachin amber from Myanmar. The study published in the journal Insects , also revealed an extraordinary biological adaptation that characterised Noo-Noo and its close relatives, exceptionally long and flexible mouthparts that were twice the length of their body. The researchers believe that this unusual structure enabled the insects to reach food sources that were inaccessible to insects with more rigid mouthparts, deep inside cracks and crevices in tree bark. In their modern relatives, the mouthparts are structured like a simple needle, allowing them to pierce plant tissues and suck fluids from them.The ancient insects examined were found to possess extremely elongated mouthparts, the surface of which was densely covered with transverse folds.Using high-resolution micro-computed tomography, the researchers were able to reconstruct their internal structure. The scans showed that the folds were not merely external ornamentation but part of the structure itself. They likely gave the mouthparts flexibility while preventing them from kinking or collapsing, much like a bendy drinking straw or a corrugated flexible hose.In some of the preserved fossils, the mouthparts were preserved in a bent position. Because the amber froze the insects in place when they became trapped in the resin, the researchers view this as further evidence that the mouthparts were also flexible during the insects' lifetimes. Such a structure is unknown among their living relatives today, pointing to an ancient evolutionary solution that has since disappeared.The mouthparts of "Noo-Noo" pointed backwards and functioned as a piercing-and-sucking system that, like the mouthparts of their modern relatives, was less suitable for feeding on nectar. Moreover, despite examining numerous fossils, the researchers found no convincing evidence of pollen accumulating on their bodies, a sign that would have indicated a role as pollinators.According to an explanation proposed by the researchers, these insects were specialists in sucking sap from trees. Their long, flexible mouthparts could have snaked through narrow cracks in the bark and guided the piercing organs toward the deep vascular tissues.At the tip was another unusual feature: a structure with two grooved lobes that likely opened during feeding, helping to anchor the mouthpart to the walls of the crack, much like a wall anchor expanding inside a drilled hole.The researchers' discovery may also have broader significance for the understanding of Cretaceous forests. Long or corrugated feeding structures appeared in several unrelated insect groups during this period, raising the possibility that forests rich in thick-barked trees provided an advantage for insects capable of reaching deeper tissues.The study notes that resin-producing forests of the Cretaceous period were also associated with evidence of recurrent fires and that trees in fire-prone environments often develop thicker bark. The researchers cautiously suggest that such conditions may have created ecological opportunities for unique feeding strategies, ones that are almost entirely absent among planthoppers today."The discovery of 'Noo-Noo,' a new species that lived approximately 99 million years ago, gives us an extraordinary glimpse into the insect world of the age of the dinosaurs. This is not merely an insect previously unknown to science, but an animal that developed an evolutionary solution with almost no modern equivalent: a long, flexible and durable feeding organ that likely enabled it to reach food deep within tree bark," said Dr. Leonidas-Romanos Davranoglou of the School of Zoology, one of the study authors."The fact that similar structures appeared in several insect groups during the Cretaceous period suggests that ancient forests created ecological conditions and opportunities very different from those we know today. The discovery of a new species like this is therefore not simply the addition of another name to the tree of life, but another piece of the puzzle that enables us to reconstruct what ecosystems looked like and how they functioned tens of millions of years ago," they added.
Article Summary: New species named Cretodorus noonoo, or 'Noo-Noo,' discovered in Myanmar. Insects had extremely elongated mouthparts, the surface of which was densely covered with transverse folds. This enabled the insects to reach food sources inaccessible to insects with more rigid mouthparts.

Article Title: A Delaware homeowner representing herself won part of a default judgment against her community’s developer; the court ordered pond and ditch maintenance and disclosure of records behind an alleged $44
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

Homeowner took the case to court herself

Court orders pond and ditch maintenance

Dispute over the $44,329.59 HOA loan

Not every claim was successful

What the ruling means for the community

A Delaware homeowner who represented herself in court has secured part of the relief she sought from her community’s developer, but not everything she asked for. The court ordered the developer to address maintenance problems involving ponds and ditches and provide information and documents concerning an alleged $44,329.59 loan involving the homeowners association. According to an October 5, 2026 order from the Delaware Court of Chancery, the ruling came after the developer failed to defend the case, leading to a partial default judgment. The court’s order, in Colston v. The Greens at Wyoming Homeowners Association, Inc., also rejected some of the homeowner’s other requests, including certain books-and-records claims.The dispute involved Gwendolyn Colston, a homeowner in The Greens at Wyoming community in Delaware, and the community’s homeowners association (HOA) and developer. Colston represented herself in the litigation, meaning she proceeded without an attorney. Her lawsuit raised several issues involving the community, its homeowners association and the developer, including the condition and maintenance of ponds and drainage ditches. She also sought information concerning a $44,329.59 loan that she alleged was connected to the HOA.According to the Delaware Court of Chancery’s October 5 order, the developer failed to appear, plead or otherwise defend the case, leading Colston to seek a default judgment.A default judgment does not automatically mean every allegation made by a plaintiff is accepted or that every remedy requested must be granted. The court still has to determine what relief is legally available based on the claims and evidence before it.One of the main areas where Colston obtained relief concerned the community’s ponds and ditches. The court found that the applicable Delaware environmental provisions supported injunctive relief requiring maintenance. As a result, the developer was ordered to take steps concerning the maintenance of the community’s ponds and ditches.The order is significant because Colston had sought action over conditions affecting drainage and water-management features within the development. Rather than awarding her money for those claims, the court directed the appropriate maintenance-related relief. The distinction matters. The court specifically explained that the statutory provisions at issue allowed for injunctive relief but did not provide a private right of action for monetary damages. Therefore, Colston could obtain an order requiring action, but she could not use those provisions to secure a financial award for the alleged violations.Another part of the case focused on an alleged loan of $44,329.59. Colston sought information and documents relating to the loan, including records that could help explain the transaction and its connection to the homeowners association. The court granted relief requiring the developer to confirm whether it had taken out such a loan and, if so, provide information and documents concerning it. That gives Colston a way to obtain records that she said were relevant to understanding the HOA’s financial dealings.The loan issue was separate from the court’s ruling on the broader books-and-records claim. The court did not simply order the defendants to turn over every HOA record requested by Colston.Although Colston won important portions of the case, the ruling was not a complete victory. The court rejected her books-and-records claim because it was directed against the wrong party and did not meet the requirements under Delaware law. That means the default judgment did not give Colston everything she had sought in the lawsuit.The court's approach also illustrates the limits of a default judgment. Even when a defendant fails to contest a case, the plaintiff still has to establish a legal basis for the particular remedy being requested.For residents of The Greens at Wyoming, the order addresses practical issues involving the development’s infrastructure as well as questions surrounding an alleged HOA loan. The pond and ditch provisions could require the developer to take action to keep those features properly maintained. Meanwhile, the disclosure concerning the $44,329.59 loan could provide additional information about the financial transaction at the centre of that part of the dispute. The case also highlights how a homeowner representing herself can pursue claims in the Delaware Court of Chancery, while showing that success on one part of a lawsuit does not necessarily extend to every claim or remedy.The October 5 order therefore leaves Colston with a mixed result: she obtained court-ordered relief concerning pond and ditch maintenance and secured disclosure tied to the alleged $44,329.59 loan, but the court declined other requests. The ruling came from the Delaware Court of Chancery, which handled the dispute and determined the scope of relief available under the claims before it.
Article Summary: Gwendolyn Colston represented herself in the litigation, meaning she proceeded without an attorney. Her lawsuit raised several issues involving the community, its homeowners association and the developer, including the condition and maintenance of ponds and drainage ditches. She also sought information concerning a $44,329.59 loan that she alleged was connected to the HOA. The developer failed to defend the case, leading to a partial default judgment.

Article Title: A Florida woman rode 7,000 miles through 48 states in six days, then donated $17,560 to the house that supported her when her 2-pound newborn spent nearly three months in intensive care
Article Text:
Jess also became the fastest documented woman to complete the 48-state ride

The journey: Six days and 48 states

When Quantum House helped Jess

The 'full circle moment'

A Florida woman has completed a 7,000-mile motorcycle ride through 48 US states in six days and used the journey to raise $17,560 for Quantum House, CW34 reported on Monday. The organisation had supported her more than two decades ago when her newborn daughter spent nearly three months in hospital.The Palm Beach County woman, known as Jess Rips on social media, began the ride on May 12. She covered an average of more than 1,100 miles a day while travelling from Vermont to Washington. Her longest stretch on the road lasted 23 hours.Jess, who has been riding motorcycles since she was 18, also became the fastest documented woman to complete the 48-state ride. But the journey was not only about setting a record, but she wanted to use the attention surrounding the ride to raise money and awareness for Quantum House, a pediatric hospitality house that had helped her family during a difficult period.The connection goes back 22 years, when Jess's daughter was born weighing just two pounds and one ounce. The baby spent nearly three months at St Mary's Medical Center, and there were days when doctors were unsure whether she would survive. During that period, Quantum House gave Jess somewhere to stay close to her daughter.Jess said she set herself a target of completing the motorcycle journey in six days. “I started on May 12th of this year, 2026, and the goal was six days,” she said as quoted by CW34.Completing that schedule meant spending long hours on the motorcycle every day. She averaged more than 1,100 miles daily, while her longest single-day ride kept her on the road for 23 hours. “It was exhausting,” Jess said. “Between the weather changes, the traffic, it was a lot mentally and physically,” she said. Despite the difficult conditions, she completed the 7,000-mile journey within her six-day target.Jess had expected the unusual challenge to attract attention, particularly online, and decided before starting that she wanted to turn that interest towards Quantum House. “When I thought about doing this ride, and I knew it was something that was so crazy that people were going to get pumped about, especially online, I thought that this would just be a great opportunity to raise awareness for this,” she said.Twenty-two years earlier, Jess' daughter had been born weighing two pounds and one ounce and remained at St Mary's Medical Center for nearly three months. “There were many days where they called me, and they didn't know if she was going to make it,” Jess recalled.Quantum House provided Jess with a place to stay while her daughter was receiving treatment. That meant she could remain close to the hospital without facing the additional financial pressure of arranging accommodation.For Jess, however, the support went beyond having somewhere to sleep. She was also surrounded by other parents facing similar situations.“It was such an amazing experience because not only was I able to stay here and it relieved that financial burden on my family, but I was also provided other families and mothers that were going through the same thing and it gave me the opportunity to have somebody to talk to,” she said.The organisation continues to help families by taking care of practical needs while their children are receiving medical care.“For the families that come here, it reduces such a burden when it comes to cost,” Quantum House President and CEO Greg Quattlebaum said. “It’s a place where they can stay and they don't have to worry about where they sleep, where they wash their clothes, what am I going to eat, where do I socialize, how do I take care of all those social determinants of health, Quantum House does that,” he adds.The motorcycle journey eventually raised $17,560 for Quantum House. When Jess returned to present the cheque, she brought both of her daughters with her. That included the daughter whose birth had first brought her to Quantum House more than two decades earlier. “So she got to see where I stayed at when I was caring for her and that was really a full circle moment,” Jess said..Her 7,000-mile journey, including the difficulties and setbacks she faced while trying to finish the ride, was also documented on her YouTube channel, Rips Unfiltered.
Article Summary: Palm Beach County woman, known as Jess Rips on social media, began the ride on May 12. She covered an average of more than 1,100 miles a day while travelling from Vermont to Washington. Her longest stretch on the road lasted 23 hours. Jess also became the fastest documented woman to complete the 48-state ride.

Moscow under drone swarm: Ukraine launches massive overnight attack

Ukraine launched an overnight drone attack involving around 650 drones targeting the Moscow region, Russian authorities said on Tuesday, in one of the largest such attacks on the Russian capital and its surroundings in the past two years.Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 105 drones were downed near the city. Article Title: From 1946, NSW planted South African bitou bush to stabilise coastal sand dunes; decades later it had spread along 46% of the state's coastline and threatened native ecosystems
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

A plant brought in to stabilise dunes

How bitou bush spread

Native plants and animals face pressure

Efforts now focus on containment and restoration

A plant introduced with a practical purpose along the New South Wales (NSW) coast eventually became a major environmental weed. South African bitou bush was deliberately planted along the NSW coastline between 1946 and 1968 to help stabilise sand dunes, according to the NSW Environment and Heritage department. The fast-growing shrub later spread rapidly and is now found along 46% of the state's coastline, with some infestations extending up to 10 kilometres inland. What was once used to control shifting sand has since become a threat to native coastal vegetation and wildlife, prompting long-running efforts to contain and remove it.Bitou bush, scientifically known as Chrysanthemoides monilifera subsp. rotundata, is native to South Africa. NSW Environment and Heritage says it is thought to have initially reached Australia in ship ballast before later being deliberately used for dune stabilisation. Its deliberate planting along the NSW coast began in 1946 and continued through 1968. The plant was valued because it grew quickly and could help hold loose coastal sand in place. Historical government documents also record its use to stabilise and revegetate dunes affected by coastal sand mining.Planting took place at a number of coastal locations, including Ballina, Byron Bay, Crescent Head, Iluka, Lake Munmorah, Port Macquarie, Redhead, The Entrance and Tweed Heads. The same characteristics that made bitou bush useful for stabilisation, however, also helped it become difficult to control once it established beyond planted areas.Once established along the coastline, bitou bush spread through a combination of deliberate planting and natural expansion. The NSW government now records it along 46% of the state's coastline, with the north coast particularly heavily affected. In some locations, the shrub has moved as far as 10 kilometres inland. Bitou bush is capable of growing rapidly and forming dense stands. Rather than simply occupying empty spaces, it can move into existing coastal plant communities and create thick shrub layers.That expansion has changed the character of some dunes, headlands and other coastal habitats. Earlier government assessments described an even wider distribution at different points in time, reflecting differences in surveys, definitions and assessment periods. A NSW Scientific Committee determination in 1999, for example, reported the weed on 90% of the state's sandy coast. The current NSW Environment and Heritage data shows the figure as 46% of the state's coastline.The main environmental concern is not simply the presence of an introduced shrub but what happens when it becomes dominant. According to NSW Environment and Heritage, bitou bush invades coastal heathlands, grasslands, woodlands and forests. It can form dense stands that replace native plants and alter habitats used by native animals. Infestations can also smother vegetation communities found on sand dunes and headlands.The NSW Bitou Threat Abatement Plan identified 157 native plant species, three plant populations and 24 ecological communities as being at risk from bitou bush and boneseed invasion. The plan also identified 24 native animal species potentially threatened by the spread of the weeds. Because of these impacts, the NSW Scientific Committee has listed the invasion of native plant communities by bitou bush and boneseed as a key threatening process affecting native plants and animals.Managing the weed is now a long-term conservation task. Bitou bush and the related South African plant boneseed were collectively listed as Weeds of National Significance in 2000. NSW has also developed a Threat Abatement Plan that directs control towards sites where removing the weed can provide the greatest benefit to threatened species and ecological communities.The approach involves more than simply removing individual plants. Control programmes involve government agencies, local authorities, community groups, Aboriginal groups, land managers and bush regenerators. The NSW plan identifies 169 priority sites, alongside northern and southern containment zones intended to limit further spread and protect important native vegetation.Under the NSW Biosecurity Act 2015, specific requirements also apply to bitou bush management. In areas north of Cape Byron and south of Point Perpendicular, eradication is required, while the central coastal distribution is managed through containment measures.The history of bitou bush shows how a species introduced to solve one environmental problem can create another when it spreads beyond its intended role. Decades after it was planted to stabilise NSW sand dunes, the shrub has become widespread enough to require coordinated control, with restoration efforts now aimed at giving native coastal ecosystems space to recover. The continuing challenge is to prevent further spread while gradually restoring the native vegetation and habitats that have been affected by the invasive plant, a process that is likely to require sustained monitoring and management for years to come.
Article Summary: South African bitou bush was deliberately planted along the NSW coastline between 1946 and 1968. The fast-growing shrub later spread rapidly and is now found along 46% of the state's coastline. In some locations, the shrub has moved as far as 10 kilometres inland. Infestations can smother vegetation communities found on sand dunes and headlands.

Article Title: How flydubai security failure, across 3 countries, almost led to 'Israel’s 9/11’
Article Text:
File photo: A flydubai aircraft at Ben Gurion International Airport

Oman flagged him, but the warning did not travel

Hammam al-Hammami

Israel had his name, and still let him fly

The cockpit attack

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is most important for improving airline security? Cross-Border Intelligence Sharing Stronger Background Checks for Crew Better Security Checks at Airports Stronger Cockpit Security & Access Control 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

A string of security failures across Oman, the UAE and Israel allowed the flydubai co-pilot to get into the cockpit, a Wall Street Journal investigation has found. The lapses nearly led to an aviation disaster reminiscent of 9/11, despite authorities having reasons to be concerned about him.The failures began in Oman, where authorities had scrutinised Hamam al-Hammami’s online activity and found he showed too much interest in radical ideology to be trusted as a pilot at state carrier Oman Air. They banned him from flying, sent him to a deradicalisation programme and moved him to a desk job, but did not broadly communicate their concerns about him.When al-Hammami joined flydubai in February, the airline did not contact Oman to vet his previous experience, the WSJ reported. It conducted a criminal-background check, but the earlier concerns that had led Oman to remove him from flying were not passed on to the new employer. The operator, flydubai, later assigned him to the sensitive Tel Aviv route, which he flew multiple times.Oman’s handling of the case also created another missed opportunity. People familiar with the matter said that had the country formally withdrawn al-Hammami’s pilot licence over its concerns, the action would likely have been flagged to the UAE.Instead, the concerns about his extremism were not communicated more widely.The final layer of failures came in Israel, where foreign airlines are required to submit passenger and crew lists before arriving.Airline operator flydubai had submitted the manifest for Flight 1073, but Israel’s transportation ministry said it did not believe it had the authority or expertise to vet foreign flight crews. The ministry also said it had never asked to access a database created in 2023 to help authorised agencies review passenger and crew information because it did not know the database was operational or that it could use it.There was an even more basic warning that should have stopped al-Hammami from flying to Israel. Pilots from countries such as Oman, which does not have diplomatic relations with Israel, are barred from flying to the country. Yet al-Hammami was allowed onto the Tel Aviv-bound flight.Israel’s own previous warnings also raise questions about how the system failed. A classified May 2024 report by the country’s comptroller general had warned that aviation security had grown lax, with fragmented responsibilities and unclear lines of authority. The report also identified manpower and budget problems affecting oversight by the transportation ministry.The security failures culminated halfway through Flight 1073, when al-Hammami attacked Captain Smit Machchhar with an emergency axe after excusing himself to pray.The wounded captain managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and others to enter and overpower the co-pilot. They then helped pull the aircraft out of a dangerous dive.The UAE’s attorney general has described the incident as an attempted terrorist act. Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Israel suspect al-Hammami was trying to crash the aircraft in Tel Aviv, according to people familiar with their thinking. All three countries are investigating whether he acted alone; so far, investigators have not found links to a foreign power or major terrorist organisation, those people said.The incident has since prompted Israel to review the security of foreign airline flights to the country.
Article Summary: Oman Air banned Hamam al-Hammami from flying, but did not communicate concerns about him to flydubai. The airline did not contact Oman to vet his previous experience. Israel’s transportation ministry said it did not believe it had the authority or expertise to vet foreign flight crews.

Article Title: Russia plague scare puts US on watch as Rubio flags possible internal spread
Article Text:
US monitors suspected plague case in Russian lab worker amid fears of internal spread, says Rubio

The United States is closely monitoring a suspected plague infection involving a laboratory worker in Russia amid concerns that the disease may have spread internally, US secretary of state Marco Rubio said, while stressing that Washington's information on the case is based on details provided by Russian officials.Rubio made the remarks while speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews before departing for a European visit. He said the US was aware of the case through information provided by Russian officials and was closely watching the situation over concerns that the infection could have spread internally.Rubio said the information available to Washington indicated that a worker at a Russian laboratory had been infected and that there was concern the infection may have spread within the facility.“We don't - we know what we know, obviously, about whatever the Russians have provided, which is it seems that there was a worker at the lab that was infected, and there's concern that that could have spread, at least internally,” he said.Rubio also indicated that quarantine measures had been taken in connection with the incident, although he did not provide details about the number of people affected or whether any internal transmission had been confirmed.He noted that travel between the US and Russia was currently limited, but said an infection that escapes its initial setting could spread quickly. “There's very limited travel between the US and Russia, obviously. But like anything else, something like that gets out, it could quickly spread,” he said.The remarks came after a laboratory worker at Russia's Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute died following pneumonia of unknown origin, prompting quarantine and medical monitoring of her contacts. Russian authorities have not confirmed plague as the cause of death, although reports have raised the possibility of pneumonic plague.Reports also alleged that the worker may have been exposed to plague bacteria in a laboratory incident, but Russian authorities have denied evidence of an accident involving dangerous pathogens. Authorities have identified the known contacts and reported no new cases among institute staff.There is also no confirmation that the worker had pneumonic plague or that human-to-human transmission occurred.
Article Summary: US monitoring suspected plague case in Russian lab worker amid fears of internal spread, says Rubio. US secretary of state says Washington's information on the case is based on details provided by Russian officials. A laboratory worker at Russia's Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute died following pneumonia.

Article Title: Kristin Davis helped rescue one-year-old elephant after finding her alone in Kenya; years later, Chaimu returned to the wild and inspired a sculpture
Article Text:
Sheldrick Wildlife Trust

Kristin Davis helps rescue an abandoned elephant calf in Kenya

From the nursery to Tsavo East: Chaimu learns life among wild elephants

PC: Sheldrick Wildlife Trust

A 2011 Kenya visit strengthens Davis’s ties to elephant conservation

A longer commitment to wildlife conservation

Chaimu becomes part of a larger conservation project

From an orphaned calf to life in the wild

In 2009, a holiday in Kenya brought actress Kristin Davis into an unexpected encounter with an abandoned elephant calf. While staying in the Chyulu Hills, Davis and staff from Kampi Ya Kanzi came across the young elephant on its own. When the calf was still without its mother several days later, a decision was made to intervene. The orphan, later named Chaimu, was about a year old and was taken into the care of the David Sheldrick Wildlife Trust, now known as the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust. Sixteen years on, Chaimu has become part of a very different story. After years of rehabilitation and time learning alongside wild elephants, she has returned to the wild.Davis was holidaying in the Chyulu Hills when she and people working at Kampi Ya Kanzi spotted the calf. At first, there was uncertainty over whether the elephant had simply become separated from its herd. But the situation did not change over the following days.With the calf continuing to remain alone, the group decided that intervention was necessary. The DSWT was contacted and arrangements were made to rescue the young elephant.She was named Chaimu and, at roughly one year old, began a rehabilitation process that would eventually take her from the Nairobi Nursery to the organisation’s reintegration programme in Tsavo East.Chaimu’s care did not end with her arrival at the Nairobi Nursery. Orphaned elephants in rehabilitation need to develop many of the behaviours they would ordinarily learn from their families, including how to interact with other elephants and function within a herd.After graduating from the nursery, Chaimu moved to the Ithumba Reintegration Centre in Tsavo East. The centre allows older orphan elephants to spend increasing amounts of time around wild elephants before making the transition away from human care.That process was reflected in Davis’s later descriptions of Chaimu. The elephant was regularly mixing with wild herds and learning the skills needed for life outside the sanctuary system.The encounter did not become an isolated episode in Davis’s life. She continued supporting the organisation and used her public profile to draw attention to its work with orphaned elephants and wider conservation issues.Her involvement included visits to Kenya. In July 2011, she returned with her friend Ame and filmmaker Roz Edwards, spending time at the Nairobi Nursery before travelling to Ithumba in Tsavo East. During that visit, she stayed at Ithumba Camp, which had been established alongside the reintegration centre and was intended to support limited responsible tourism in the northern part of Tsavo East.Davis also spoke publicly about Chaimu and the charity’s work, including an appearance on The Oprah Winfrey Show. She has continued to identify elephant conservation and the illegal ivory trade among the issues she has highlighted.Davis’s work with elephants has since extended beyond her connection with Chaimu. She also served as a Goodwill Ambassador for UNHCR, the UN Refugee Agency, in 2017, according to The UN Refugee Agency.Her interest in conservation has also crossed into film. The Perfect World Foundation Award says that in 2014, she executive produced and financed Gardeners of Eden, a documentary about the Sheldrick Wildlife Trust and its efforts to protect elephants. The film received recognition at several film festivals, including the Elephant Hero Award at the UN-sponsored International Elephant Film Festival in 2016, and was later a finalist for a Peabody Award.In September 2023, Davis received The Perfect World Foundation Award for her contribution to raising awareness around wildlife and biodiversity conservation.Years after the original rescue, Chaimu’s story became connected to The Great Elephant Migration, a conservation art project involving a travelling collection of elephant sculptures. Davis has supported the project and said she wanted to help raise awareness and funds for conservation work.A sculpture representing Chaimu is part of the migrating herd. Its inclusion links the animal Davis encountered as an orphaned calf in Kenya with the elephant she later saw progressing through rehabilitation and towards life in the wild.By then, Chaimu was 16 years old and had been reintegrated into the wild. Her story therefore spans much more than the original rescue. It covers the long period between being found alone in the Chyulu Hills and eventually becoming capable of living beyond the protection of the rehabilitation programme.Chaimu’s journey illustrates the lengthy nature of elephant rehabilitation. The rescue itself happened quickly once it became clear that the calf was not being reunited with her herd, but the process that followed took years.From the Nairobi Nursery to Ithumba, Chaimu gradually spent more time in an environment where wild elephants could provide experiences and social interactions that a young orphan would otherwise have gained from its family. Her eventual return to the wild marked the later stage of that process.For Davis, the connection began with an encounter during a Kenyan holiday in 2009. More than a decade later, Chaimu’s name remains attached to her conservation work, this time through a sculpture travelling with The Great Elephant Migration and representing an elephant that survived the loss of its original herd and went on to rejoin wild elephants.
Article Summary: Kristin Davis came across an abandoned elephant calf in Kenya in 2009. The calf, later named Chaimu, was taken into the care of the David Sheldrick Wildlife Trust. Davis continued supporting the organisation and used her public profile to draw attention to its work with orphaned elephants and wider conservation issues.

Article Title: A Michigan homeowner owed $3,000 in taxes, but the county sold her home and kept all $23,500; an appeals court has now reopened her legal fight to recover the surplus from the foreclosure
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

How the foreclosure dispute began

The class-action case that changed the timeline

Why the county said the lawsuit was too late

What the appeals court decided

The question still left for the lower court

What happens next

A $3,000 tax debt ended with a Michigan homeowner losing her home and the county keeping $23,500 from its sale. Years later, her fight to recover that money is back in court. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit, in an October 5, 2026 opinion in Cunningham v. Allegan County, overturned a lower-court dismissal and sent the case back for further proceedings. The court said the lower court used the wrong legal approach when deciding whether Denise Thompson’s federal claim was filed too late. The ruling does not mean Thompson has won the $23,500; instead, it gives her lawsuit another chance to move forward.Thompson’s case stems from Michigan’s former tax-foreclosure system. Counties could foreclose on properties when owners failed to pay their property taxes, sell those properties and, under the system in place at the time, keep the money left over after the tax debt was satisfied. That is what happened to Thompson, according to the Sixth Circuit. She owed about $3,000 in taxes, but Allegan County foreclosed on her home and later sold it.The county kept the entire $23,500 in sale proceeds, an amount substantially higher than the debt that triggered the foreclosure.Thompson was not the only homeowner affected. Gary and Josette Day also lost property through Allegan County foreclosures in 2013 and 2014. Their claims eventually became part of a broader legal battle over whether Michigan counties could retain surplus money generated by tax-foreclosure sales.In December 2014, Michigan taxpayers filed a class action known as Wayside Church v. County of Van Buren. The plaintiffs argued that counties violated the Constitution’s Takings Clause by keeping surplus proceeds after selling foreclosed properties. Thompson and the Days were unnamed members of the plaintiff class, while Allegan County was initially an unnamed member of the defendant class. The lawsuit was dismissed in 2015 but reopened in 2019 after developments in the law.In July 2023, Thompson and the Days opted out of a class settlement because they wanted to pursue individual claims against Allegan County. They filed those lawsuits in March 2024. That timing became the central issue in the case.Allegan County argued that Thompson and the Days had missed the deadline for bringing their federal claims. The district court agreed and dismissed the claims as time-barred. The homeowners, however, argued that their participation in the Wayside class action had paused the statute of limitations. They had remained part of that litigation for more than eight years and argued that the clock should not have been running against them throughout that entire period. The Sixth Circuit agreed that the lower court had taken the wrong approach.Judge Amul Thapar, writing for the Sixth Circuit, said Michigan law controls the tolling issue because the homeowners brought their claims under federal civil-rights law, but such claims generally borrow the applicable state statute of limitations. The court found that Michigan’s tolling rules could apply to the Wayside litigation. It also concluded that the 2019 reopening of the class action meant the tolling period could continue rather than simply ending when the case was dismissed in 2015.That matters because, if the Wayside case paused the clock until Thompson and the Days opted out, their individual lawsuits could have been filed within the applicable deadline. But the appeals court did not decide that the claims are definitely timely.The Sixth Circuit said another issue needs to be examined: whether Allegan County had sufficient notice of the claims while it was still an unnamed member of the proposed defendant class. Michigan law generally allows class-action tolling when defendants have notice of the claims and the general identities of the potential plaintiffs. But the appeals court said the existing record does not clearly establish when Allegan County received that notice.Because that question could determine whether Thompson’s claim survives, the Sixth Circuit vacated the district court’s dismissal and sent the case back for further proceedings.The ruling does not order Allegan County to pay Thompson the $23,500. Instead, it keeps her legal fight alive and requires the lower court to examine the notice and tolling issues again. The case also sits within a much larger Michigan dispute over foreclosure surpluses. In 2020, the Michigan Supreme Court ruled in Rafaeli, LLC v. Oakland County that counties’ retention of surplus proceeds after satisfying a property-tax debt violated the Michigan Constitution’s Takings Clause. Litigation has continued over how those principles apply to older foreclosures and how former homeowners can seek repayment.For Thompson, the immediate question is more specific: whether the earlier class action paused the legal deadline for her claim. If it did, her effort to recover the $23,500 surplus can continue.
Article Summary: Denise Thompson owed about $3,000 in taxes, but Allegan County foreclosed on her home and later sold it. The county kept the entire $23,500 in sale proceeds, an amount substantially higher than the debt that triggered the foreclosure. Thompson and the Days opted out of a class settlement because they wanted to pursue individual claims.

Article Title: Meryl Streep made a seven-figure gift to preserve women's history; the museum is using it to bring stories into classrooms and digital media
Article Text:
Meryl Streep backs a wider effort to preserve women’s history

The museum is putting digital storytelling at the centre

Bringing women’s history into classrooms

Meryl Streep has backed the museum since its early years

The museum’s plans extend beyond the physical space

Looking towards the United States’ 250th anniversary

Meryl Streep has made a seven-figure gift to the National Women’s History Museum as the institution prepares to expand how women’s stories are taught and shared across the United States. The donation will support digital projects designed to take historical material beyond a traditional museum setting, including resources that can be used in classrooms and accessed through online platforms. Streep has been a supporter of the museum making the contribution part of a longer association with its work. The museum is also establishing an annual educator award in her name, with the first recipient due to be recognised in November 2026.Streep has supported the National Women’s History Museum for years, making the new contribution an extension of an existing relationship rather than a first association with the institution. Meryl Streep said, “History is shaped not only by those who make it, but by those who ensure it is remembered.”“The National Women’s History Museum has long been a catalyst for bringing forward the stories that deepen our understanding of who we are.I am proud to continue supporting this essential work so that future generations inherit a history that is both truthful and complete.”For an institution whose purpose is to bring women’s contributions into the historical record, the timing also has a practical significance. The museum is preparing to increase its national impact ahead of the United States’ 250th anniversary, when questions about which people and events are represented in the country’s history are likely to receive renewed attention.A substantial part of the funding will go towards digital-first projects. The aim is to create material that does not depend on someone physically visiting a museum or exhibition to encounter it. That could mean resources being used in a classroom, viewed at home or encountered through the digital services people already use. The museum has described the approach as a way of making its storytelling more flexible and accessible, particularly as it seeks to reach audiences outside its established base. The shift also reflects the practical limits of a traditional museum model. Physical exhibitions can only be visited in particular places and at particular times. Digital resources can travel much further, allowing historical material to be used by teachers and students who may never visit the museum itself.For the National Women’s History Museum, the new funding provides an opportunity to develop that side of its work on a larger scale.Education is another clear focus of Streep’s contribution. The museum plans to use its expanded resources to make women’s history more available to teachers, students and communities across the country.The institution will also create the Meryl Streep Educator Award. It will be given each year to an educator whose work advances the teaching of women’s history and makes those stories more accessible in schools or local communities. The first recipient is due to be recognised at the museum’s Women Making History Awards Gala in November 2026. The award gives the donation a direct connection to education rather than leaving it solely as a funding commitment for digital development. It also creates an annual way for the museum to recognise teachers whose work brings historical material into everyday learning.Streep’s involvement with the National Women’s History Museum predates the latest donation. The museum has identified her as one of its earliest and most consistent supporters. Her own career has also been closely associated with portraying women in film, although the museum’s recognition of her is centred on her support for its educational and historical mission. In announcing the gift, its leadership linked her work as an actor and storyteller with the broader role of preserving and communicating women’s experiences.Susan D. Whiting, chair of the museum’s board, described Streep’s contribution as consistent with the organisation’s emphasis on education, historical representation and access to women’s stories. Streep said the museum helps bring forward accounts that can add to a fuller understanding of the past. Her latest contribution, she said, was intended to support that work for future generations.“As one of the most influential storytellers of our time, Meryl Streep has spent her career illuminating the depth, complexity, and power of women’s lives.”The National Women’s History Museum has increasingly looked towards digital methods as a way of reaching people beyond a conventional museum audience. The new funding is expected to give those efforts more room to develop. That means the museum’s work will not be limited to presenting information in one location. A teacher could use its material during a lesson, a student could encounter it while researching a subject, and someone at home could explore the same stories independently.The approach also gives the museum more scope to tell stories in different formats. Digital platforms can combine written material with visual storytelling and other forms of presentation, allowing historical subjects to be approached in ways that may not fit easily within a physical exhibition.Frédérique Campagne Irwin, the museum’s president and CEO said, “Meryl Streep understands that storytelling shapes culture, and culture shapes what societies believe is possible.”The museum is planning its expansion against the backdrop of the United States’ 250th anniversary in 2026. That milestone provides a particular moment for institutions concerned with how American history is recorded and taught.For the National Women’s History Museum, the anniversary is being treated as an opportunity to bring more attention to women whose contributions have formed part of the country’s history. The new investment is intended to help the museum do that on a national scale rather than relying primarily on visitors who can reach a physical museum setting.
Article Summary: Meryl Streep has made a seven-figure gift to the National Women’s History Museum. The donation will support digital projects designed to take historical material beyond a traditional museum setting. The museum is also establishing an annual educator award in her name, with the first recipient due to be recognised in November 2026.

Article Title: A $2.35 million security project at North Dakota’s governor’s residence uncovered human remains; archaeologists have now removed 7 coffins after examining more than 80 areas around the construction si
Article Text:
The discovery dates back to May, when workers installing a new fence near the governor’s residence encountered human remains. The location was once part of Bismarck’s first cemetery, which operated between 1873 and 1877.

A cemetery beneath modern Bismarck

A careful examination of the remains

Not the first discovery in the area

Preparing for a respectful reburial

An unexpected cost to a security project

A routine security upgrade at North Dakota’s governor’s residence has opened an unexpected window into Bismarck’s past. What began as a $2.35 million project to improve fencing and access around the property turned into an archaeological investigation after construction crews uncovered human remains beneath the ground, states an online report by North Dakota Monitor. Months later, archaeologists have removed seven coffins containing human remains, along with an unidentified wooden box, after examining more than 80 areas of interest around the construction site, the report adds.The discovery dates back to May, when workers installing a new fence near the governor’s residence encountered human remains. The location was once part of Bismarck’s first cemetery, which operated between 1873 and 1877. Many of the people originally buried there were later moved to St. Mary’s Cemetery and Fairview Cemetery during the 1880s. The discovery suggests that some burials may have remained behind despite those historic efforts to relocate graves, the report adds.Archaeologists returned to the area in September for a more extensive investigation. Their work covered more than 80 areas identified as potentially significant, eventually leading to the removal of the seven coffins and the wooden box.The findings add another layer to the history of a part of the city that has undergone substantial development since the cemetery was active, adds the report.The archaeological work is now moving into its next phase. Researchers will examine and catalogue the remains and other objects recovered during the fieldwork, a process expected to continue into early 2027. The analysis is expected to focus on basic biological information such as estimated age ranges and possible evidence of disease or other conditions that might provide clues to the individuals buried there.DNA testing is not planned as part of the investigation. Instead, archaeologists will rely on physical examination and historical research to better understand the remains and the circumstances surrounding the burials. The unidentified wooden box recovered alongside the coffins will also be examined as researchers work to establish a clearer picture of what was once located on the site.Human remains have been uncovered elsewhere around the North Dakota Capitol grounds over the decades, claims the online report. Previous discoveries occurred during construction of a trolley line near the southwest corner of the Capitol property in 1903. Remains were also found in 1959 while the previous governor’s residence was being constructed. The latest discovery therefore forms part of a longer archaeological story beneath the modern government complex, where layers of Bismarck’s early history remain hidden below later development.Authorities are taking steps to ensure the recovered remains are handled appropriately. The state has contracted with a local funeral home, while Crisis Care Chaplaincy has offered support during the process. Once the archaeological examination is complete, the remains are expected to be reinterred at a local cemetery in spring, adds the report.The reburial will provide a final resting place for people whose original graves were effectively lost beneath the changing landscape of the city.The archaeological discovery has also added an unforeseen expense to the governor’s residence project. Lawmakers approved $2.35 million last year for security improvements, including a new perimeter fence and an extension to the driveway.By September 1, archaeological work associated with the discovery was estimated to have cost the state an additional $155,000. The Office of Management and Budget has not yet provided an updated figure following completion of the exhumation work.Images Courtesy: istock and North Dakota Monitor
Article Summary: The discovery dates back to May, when workers installing a new fence near the governor’s residence encountered human remains. The location was once part of Bismarck's first cemetery, which operated between 1873 and 1877. Archaeologists have removed seven coffins containing human remains, along with an unidentified wooden box, after examining more than 80 areas of interest. The remains are expected to be reinterred at a local cemetery in spring.

Article Title: In 1994, a golfer paid $5 for a green jacket at a Toronto thrift store; it was later confirmed as an authentic 1950s Augusta National club jacket, and it sold at auction in 2017 for $139,349
Article Text:
A $5 find

Augusta National identifies the jacket

$5 jacket auctioned for $139,349

A golfer was browsing through a Toronto thrift store when he came across a green jacket. The item looked interesting, and he knew this was an unusual find. It was priced at $5, so he bought it anyway.More than two decades later, the same jacket was sold for $139,349 at auction after Augusta National Golf Club confirmed that it was an authentic club jacket dating to the 1950s, Global News reported.The jacket was later known as a ‘thrift-store Masters jacket’, an unusual piece of golf memorabilia offered by Green Jacket Auctions in 2017.An avid golfer and a member of the Canadian media discovered the jacket while browsing through a Toronto second-hand shop in 1994. He recognised the Augusta National branding and decided to buy it. He paid just $5 for the jacket, unaware of just how valuable it could eventually become. At the time, the jacket had no name, so its history remained unclear. But a tag on the jacket indicated that it dated to the 1950s. The jacket was later sold to a British golf journalist, who kept it for years before it eventually appeared at auction.The green jacket turned out to be an authentic Augusta National club jacket.Augusta National confirmed its authenticity. The green jacket is one of the most recognisable symbols in golf, and it is closely associated with Augusta National and the Masters Tournament.Members of the Georgia club wear these distinctive jackets, and the Masters winner traditionally receives one after winning the tournament. So they finalised that this jacket was a club member's jacket, not one awarded to a Masters champion.During the auction, everything about the jacket, from its age and link to Augusta National to its unusual journey from a Toronto thrift store, made it a fascinating piece of golf memorabilia.During the Spring 2017 golf-memorabilia sale, Green Jacket Auctions included this jacket. The auction featured a collection of historically significant Masters items.The bidding for this jacket began at $5,000 and attracted 34 bids before closing at $139,349.“We are blown away by the interest in golf memorabilia right now. The golf-collecting hobby has never been so strong. Yet, when you look at golf memorabilia compared to baseball and other sports, golf is selling at a relative bargain. Surely because of this we’re starting to see ‘smart’ money enter the hobby. Wealthy New Yorkers and international buyers who want the very best pieces are willing to pay what are record prices for the golf hobby because they believe that there is still a great deal of upside with the top pieces of memorabilia,” Ryan Carey, an attorney who is one of the two principals at Green Jacket Auctions, which was established in 2006, told Golf Digest.The buyer was a private collector from the United States. Green Jacket Auctions did not disclose the person's identity.For the person who found the jacket at the thrift store, this sale was nothing less than a lottery. A jacket bought for $5 had become a six-figure collector's item.Despite being sold for $139,349, this green jacket was far from the most expensive green jacket ever sold. Yes, you read that right. Back in 2013, a green jacket reportedly belonging to Horton Smith, who won the first Masters Tournament in 1934 and won again in 1936, was sold for $682,229. This 2017 sale, however, showed how much collectors were willing to pay for rare pieces of Masters history.
Article Summary: A golfer bought the jacket for $5 at a Toronto thrift store in 1994. Augusta National Golf Club confirmed it was an authentic club jacket. The jacket was later known as a 'thrift-store Masters jacket' It was auctioned by Green Jacket Auctions in 2017 for $139,349.

Article Title: In 1968, Jeff McKissack began building Houston’s Orange Show from salvaged materials, creating a unique folk art landmark that opened to the public in 1979
Article Text:
PC: Wikipedia

How did McKissack build the Orange Show

PC: Texas Monthly interview

Why did Harithas support the Orange Show

How large was the Orange Show

In October 1977, William Martin wrote in Texas Monthly that the Orange Show, a folk art site on Munger Street in southeast Houston, was the passion of its creator, Jeff McKissack, then 75. McKissack told William Martin in a Texas Monthly interview, "I work on it every day." The complex, built from salvaged materials, honours oranges, which McKissack saw as symbols of strength, purity and the American way. McKissack opened the show to the public in 1979, and it is now a pilgrimage destination for folk art lovers worldwide. This article traces its creation, collection, recognition and preservation.McKissack built the show largely from salvaged and bought items. Some came from buildings demolished in downtown Houston during his years at the Post Office. They included roof tiles from the old Capitol Theatre, a railing from a Stowers Furniture Company fire escape and a miniature obelisk from the Texas State Hotel. Other pieces came from antique and junk shops between Houston and Hot Springs, Arkansas, where McKissack had holidayed since 1918.Cast-iron tractor seats and dozens of buggy wheels were his most successful finds, and they served as seating and as decoration on gates, fences and partitions.The exhibits described included a steamboat display, a steam buggy and an exhibit room roughly eight feet wide and twenty feet long. The room held mannequin scenes, a tepee and signs with McKissack's own wording. McKissack told Martin he had at least $10,000 worth of further exhibits stored in his living room. He also said that he had worked on the project since 1968: "I started working on it in 1968, and I work on it every day. "James Harithas, director of the Contemporary Arts Museum, first visited the Orange Show in 1975 and became an enthusiastic supporter. Harithas said he took visitors to see it, among them the painter Willem de Kooning and the collector Count Panza, and called it the "Orange Shrine". His visits were interrupted when the Bicentennial flood destroyed the museum in June 1976.Harithas told Martin he doubted the show would bring McKissack substantial income unless it was sold as a work of art to a collector who would maintain it. He estimated it could fetch a few hundred thousand dollars. If no sale came about, he felt the city should take it over as a monument, and he said he intended to put the museum behind it. McKissack's own hope was for 100,000 to 300,000 visitors a year. Neighbourhood boys had broken in shortly before his last visit, pouring paint over the exhibit room and damaging exhibits. McKissack told him he had scolded the boys but had not told their parents.According to the Texas Historical Foundation, a grant presentation to the Orange Show Foundation on 27 June 2023. Working as a postal worker by day and an artist by night. By the time he opened the show to the public more than twenty years later, it said, he had assembled salvaged materials into 3,000 square feet of sculptural environment. It states that he opened it in 1979 and that it survived less than a year afterwards.The grant came from its William Jack Sibley Arts Endowment. It supports ongoing efforts to restore and maintain the site, whose oldest parts are approaching 70 years old. The foundation said the piecemeal nature of the original work makes maintenance complex, requiring fidelity to both aesthetic and structural integrity. It described the Orange Show as a pilgrimage destination for lovers of folk art around the world.
Article Summary: The Orange Show is a folk art site on Munger Street in southeast Houston. It was the passion of its creator, Jeff McKissack, then 75. The complex, built from salvaged materials, honours oranges. It is now a pilgrimage destination for folk art lovers worldwide.

Article Title: Meet Ben Hogan, former bike mechanic turning discarded bicycles into prosthetic legs; shares free instructions online to help others recreate the design locally
Article Text: A Michigan man has been turning discarded bicycles into prosthetic legs while also teaching others how to make them, all for free. Ben Hogan, a former bike mechanic and prosthetist at Mary Free Bed Rehabilitation Hospital, founded Project Bike Leg , an initiative that makes prosthetics sourced almost entirely from repurposed bike parts. He hopes his low-cost design can eventually help millions of amputees around the world, according to a report by PEOPLE's Toria Sheffield.Hogan worked at the Michigan State University Bikes Service Centre as a student 20 years ago, where he learned to repair bikes. Bike shop general manager Tim Potter trained Hogan. “When I think about it, you know, I mean, it sometimes will tear you up,” said Potter.Hogan revealed that it all began with a random encounter. “I had a chance encounter with an amputee that walked into a bike shop I was working at in Los Angeles in 2011,” he said to the outlet. “He showed me his prosthesis unprompted, and it really informed me of how much a bike and a prosthesis had in common.” “After [later] shadowing some prosthetists at UCLA, I made the connection that it was my calling,” he added.Moreover, he shared that his desire to create something both functional and cost-efficient only grew after he learned how many amputees worldwide do not have access to the prosthetics they need.Citing World Health Organisation estimates, Hogan said that a "staggering 85-90% of amputees worldwide lack access to a proper prosthesis." “As a former bike mechanic turned prosthetist, I was naturally drawn to take a bicycle and turn it into a prosthesis,” he said. “A bike, after all, is a tool used to enhance human locomotion. The inherent design would allow for an adjustable, lightweight, structurally sound and functional prosthesis.”After seriously working and experimenting with the designs, Hogan crafted his first below-the-knee prosthesis model within a few weeks in 2013. However, he said he decided to put the project aside until he had developed his skillset more fully. “Due to the fact that I had not yet achieved a master's vantage point of the prosthetic arts, I decided to set the bike leg down until I could say that I honestly had the advanced prosthetic skillset to ‘reinvent the wheel’ of prosthetic care,” he explained.It was in the summer of 2024 that he decided he was finally ready to return to the initiative, at which point he officially founded Project Bike Leg. “I had been working at Mary Free Bed Rehabilitation Hospital for the past 8 years and had a patient who was up for the challenge. Using all of the rudimentary concepts of prosthetics that I had come to know in the previous decade, I crafted a new design of a BK [below-the-knee] bike leg that had an enhanced level of adjustability and functionality compared to the previous model. ”Andy Leedom, who lost his leg five years ago in a car accident, is one of Hogan’s bike-leg testers. Leedom is on his third prosthesis, which cost nearly $70,000. “I call myself the guinea pig,” Leedom said. “Ben’s been to enough places that he knows what is needed.”He went on to design an above-the-knee model in 2025 and decided he felt ready to share his designs on a larger scale. The prosthetic is made from over 95% bicycle parts. The foot is formed from a bike seat, strips of wheel and tyre treads, held together with spokes. The seat post and frame add stability. “If you look at the back of the knee, there are two chains,” Hogan said. “These hold the knee stable and there are two of them. ”The cable used to shift gears runs around the bike-leg to hold it together. The socket is made of wicker, which local communities could make out of material they have access to. “It’s actually a perfect application for a prosthesis, because it’s already built to take the weight of a human, so all I’ve done is reconfigure it in a different way to be a prosthesis,” Hogan said.He soon met with a physician in Ghana, where he eventually travelled to personally teach prosthetics students how to recreate his designs. He shared that by the end of his nine-day trip he and the students had successfully completed their work on building two fully-made prosthetics and given two amputees the ability to walk again. “And now they can train others in the Ghana region on how to make bike legs,” Hogan said.“This was a phenomenal experience that I will never forget, and I cannot wait to see what the local clinicians might do with the bike legs moving forward,” he said of the experience.Moreover, he is training thousands more across the globe on how to make their own prosthetic legs with the help of his website. He shares instructional videos on how to make both above-the-knee and below-the-knee bike leg prosthetics, with pages of pictures and step-by-step instructions.In a recent conversation with InvestigateTV about the project, Hogan said he has no intention to patent the design or personally profit from it. “I don’t have any intention of financially benefiting from it or patenting these designs,” he told the outlet. “I want them to be available to all parties all over the world.”For Hogan, the next step is a pilot study with amputees in third-world countries wearing bike legs full time. He hopes his invention will eventually help some of the 30 to 40 million people worldwide who need prosthetic legs.“As my sister said, your career should be your greatest gift to the world,” he said, “and I do think this is my greatest gift to the world.”
Article Summary: Ben Hogan, a former bike mechanic and prosthetist at Mary Free Bed Rehabilitation Hospital, founded Project Bike Leg. The initiative makes prosthetics sourced almost entirely from repurposed bike parts. He hopes his low-cost design can eventually help millions of amputees around the world. The prosthetic is made from over 95% bicycle parts.

Article Title: Southern California once had so many of these mountain frogs that people could barely avoid stepping on them; now about 650 were released back into the wild
Article Text:
Southern mountain yellow-legged frogs make a return to mountain streams

Southern mountain yellow-legged frogs are raised under controlled conditions

Why southern mountain yellow-legged frogs are now endangered

A recovery effort involving zoos and government agencies

Southern mountain yellow-legged frogs add another 653 to a long recovery effort

In the streams of Southern California’s mountains, the southern mountain yellow-legged frog has had a difficult few decades. The species was once far more widespread, with historic accounts describing streams where frogs were so numerous that people could scarcely move without stepping around them. Finding them in the wild is a very different proposition; their remaining populations are scattered across parts of the San Gabriel, San Bernardino and San Jacinto mountains.Conservation teams released 653 captive-bred frogs into streams in the San Gabriel Mountains. The release is part of a longer recovery effort that has already returned thousands of Los Angeles Zoo-bred frogs to native habitat.According to the Association of Zoos & Aquarium (AZAs), the release happened in two stages. On 19 August, 338 southern mountain yellow-legged frogs were taken to streams in the San Gabriel Mountains and released into their native environment. A further 315 followed on 27 August, bringing the total to 653. Every frog in this release was bred at the Los Angeles Zoo. Of those, 227 had been raised in a new bio-secure amphibian headstarting facility at the zoo, a development that has expanded the number of young frogs that can be raised under controlled conditions before being returned to the mountains.The release also takes the number of Los Angeles Zoo-bred frogs returned to the wild since the Southern Mountain Yellow-legged Frog Recovery Program began to nearly 7,000.The new facility occupies a renovated section of the Los Angeles Zoo’s Children’s Discovery Center. It contains specialised tanks and life-support equipment designed to maintain suitable water conditions for the amphibians as they develop. Tadpoles can be vulnerable during their early development, so keeping them in a carefully controlled setting allows zoo staff to raise them until they are larger and more developed. They can then be released at a stage when they are better equipped to deal with predators and the other hazards found in natural streams.For the 227 frogs raised in the new facility, that process provided an expanded route from breeding and hatching to release. Byron Wusstig, curator of ectotherms at the Los Angeles Zoo said, “Seeing our new headstarting facility transition from a concept to a fully operational reality is a monumental milestone for the recovery of the southern mountain yellow-legged frog.”The work is not confined to Los Angeles. About 112 tadpoles bred at the zoo were also due to be transferred to the Santa Ana Zoo later in September for continued care.Southern mountain yellow-legged frogs are adapted to perennial streams in parts of Southern California’s mountain ranges. They are relatively small, generally measuring between about 1.5 and 3.25 inches as adults.Brown and yellow are common colours, although individuals may also appear grey, reddish or greenish-brown. Dark spots and irregular markings help them blend into surfaces around their habitat, sometimes resembling moss or lichen. The yellow or pale orange colouring on the underside of the legs is the feature behind the species' common name.Their present distribution is a shadow of the species' former presence. Historical descriptions indicate that the frogs could once occur in large numbers along Southern California mountain streams, to the point where people moving through their habitat might have struggled to avoid stepping on them.The change has been severe enough for the International Union for Conservation of Nature to classify the southern mountain yellow-legged frog as Endangered.The releases are being carried out through a partnership led by the US Geological Survey. The programme brings together the Los Angeles Zoo, San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, Omaha’s Henry Doorly Zoo and Aquarium, the US Forest Service, the US Fish and Wildlife Service and the California Department of Fish and Wildlife.Other organisations have since joined the effort, including the Aquarium of the Pacific, Santa Ana Zoo, Big Bear Alpine Zoo and Birch Aquarium at Scripps. The network is expected to expand further.For the southern mountain yellow-legged frog, the San Gabriel Mountains are one of the places where that work is now taking place.The 653 frogs released in August are not being treated as a standalone conservation event. They form part of an ongoing attempt to rebuild populations of a species that has become much less common across its former range.The Los Angeles Zoo has now contributed almost 7,000 captive-bred frogs to releases in the wild since the recovery programme began. The new headstarting facility gives the zoo another way to increase that contribution, particularly by allowing tadpoles to remain under controlled care until they reach a more suitable stage for release. The species can still be seen by visitors at the Los Angeles Zoo, where southern mountain yellow-legged frogs are displayed in the Living Amphibian, Invertebrate, and Reptile exhibit.
Article Summary: Conservation teams released 653 captive-bred frogs into streams in the San Gabriel Mountains. Every frog in this release was bred at the Los Angeles Zoo. The species was once far more widespread, with historic accounts describing streams where frogs were so numerous that people could scarcely move without stepping around them. Their present distribution is a shadow of their former presence.

Article Title: A New Jersey wildlife centre is caring for 219 box turtles after hundreds were dumped near a river; rescuers are now building outdoor enclosures so the turtles can spend winter as they would in the wi
Article Text:
Eastern box turtle (representative image)

A riverbank littered with turtles

Caring for hundreds of reptiles

Representative image

Preparing for winter with Brumation Stations

The road to release

A community rallying around wildlife

More than two months after scores of box turtles were found abandoned along a riverbank in Cranford, New Jersey, the rescue effort has entered a new phase. The Mercer County Wildlife Center now reports caring for 219 turtles connected to the July dumping, up from about 190 in early August. With colder weather approaching, the centre is building two outdoor enclosures where many of the turtles will be able to spend the winter following the same seasonal cycle they would experience in the wild. Staff have nicknamed the new habitats Brumation Stations, a reference to the reptile equivalent of hibernation. Read on to know more:The unusual rehabilitation effort began on July 29, when a Cranford resident discovered dozens of turtles abandoned along a riverbank near Riverside Drive and Casino Avenue, adjacent to the Rahway River. New Jersey Fish and Wildlife officers responded, and turtles began arriving at the Mercer County Wildlife Center in Hopewell Township and later at its River Road facility in Titusville. Residents were asked to bring any turtles they found to the Cranford Fire Department for safe transport to licensed rehabilitators, as per reports by News12 New Jersey and Abc7ny.com.The group included Eastern box turtles, which are native to New Jersey, and three-toed box turtles, a species not native to the state.Authorities have said the turtles were illegally dumped and that a law enforcement investigation is underway, but they have not announced who may have released them. Some investigators have examined whether the turtles were part of an illegal wildlife trade before being abandoned in the area. By mid-August, more than 200 box turtles had been recovered, and the Cranford Fire Department stopped accepting new turtles as the collection effort wound down. Recovered turtles were transported daily to the Mercer County Wildlife Center for treatment and evaluation. State wildlife officials said healthy Eastern box turtles would eventually be released into suitable habitat, while three-toed box turtles would be returned to wildlife agencies within their native range, as per the reports.The surge in patients put significant pressure on the Mercer County Wildlife Center, one of only three wildlife rehabilitation facilities in New Jersey permitted to care for reptiles. To handle the influx, staff and volunteers converted an entire building into temporary housing for the turtles. Every turtle has been seen by a veterinarian and is receiving a full medical workup, including triage, weight checks, X-rays, photographs, veterinary assessments, housing and feeding.Wildlife Center Director Jane Rakos-Yates said, according to The Cool Down (TCD), that each turtle requires dedicated enclosures, UV lighting, specific food and veterinary treatment, and those needs can become expensive quickly. The centre has asked supporters not to bring random produce, worms or aquariums, because the animals require very specific care. Instead, those looking to help are being encouraged to donate money or buy requested supplies through Wildlife Center Friends, the centre’s nonprofit partner.Rehabilitation manager Nicole Golden described the work as a community effort that has brought together state Fish and Wildlife officers and biologists, residents and firefighters from Cranford, local animal control officers, staffers and volunteers at the wildlife centre, the Mercer County Park Commission, veterinary specialists and members of the public, as per TCD. That broad collaboration has been essential in managing one of the biggest reptile rehabilitation efforts in the centre’s history.As autumn approaches, the focus has shifted to helping the turtles through the colder months. For healthy turtles, allowing them to follow their natural seasonal cycle is an important part of rehabilitation and can help prepare them for eventual release back into the wild, the Wildlife Center wrote in its October 3 update. With that goal in mind, the centre is constructing two outdoor enclosures where many of the turtles will be able to brumate, the reptile version of hibernation.The Brumation Stations are being built with assistance from the Mercer County Park Commission and supplies purchased with donations. The enclosures are designed to mimic the conditions the turtles would experience in the wild, with appropriate soil, shelter and protection from predators. The centre hopes to begin moving turtles into the new enclosures as early as this week, giving them time to settle in before the deepest cold sets in.Allowing the turtles to brumate outdoors serves both medical and behavioural purposes. It helps them maintain natural rhythms, supports their immune systems and reduces the stress of being kept indoors under artificial conditions for months. For a species that normally spends winter buried in leaf litter or soil, the chance to follow that pattern can improve their chances of survival after release.The long-term goal remains rehabilitation and, when possible, returning turtles to the wild. State wildlife officials have said that healthy Eastern box turtles will be released into suitable habitat after veterinary evaluations, while three-toed box turtles will be returned to wildlife agencies within their native range. That process will take time, as each turtle must be assessed for health, weight, shell condition and overall fitness before it can be considered for release.For now, the turtles remain at the Mercer County Wildlife Center, where staff continue to monitor their health and prepare them for winter. The needs of 219 turtles are ongoing, and donations help provide food, supplies, veterinary care and everything needed to keep them healthy through the colder months. The centre’s update emphasised that public support remains critical as the rehabilitation effort moves into its next phase.The Cranford turtle dumping has drawn attention far beyond the immediate rescue.
