It has highlighted the challenges wildlife rehabilitators face when confronted with large-scale illegal releases and the importance of having licensed facilities equipped to handle such incidents. The case has also underscored the role of local residents, firefighters and animal control officers in identifying and reporting abandoned animals before they suffer further harm.For neighbours along the Rahway River, the sight of hundreds of turtles scattered along the bank was both alarming and heartbreaking. Many residents stepped forward to help, searching for turtles, bringing them to collection points and supporting the wildlife centre through donations and supplies. That community response has been a bright spot in an otherwise troubling episode, showing how quickly people can mobilise when local wildlife is at risk.As the Brumation Stations take shape, the focus is shifting from emergency rescue to long-term care and eventual release. For the 219 box turtles now in human hands, the hope is that they will one day return to a safe, natural habitat where they can live out their lives as wild animals. Until then, the Mercer County Wildlife Center and its partners will continue to provide the care and protection these reptiles need to survive.
Article Summary: More than 200 box turtles were found abandoned along a riverbank in Cranford, New Jersey, on July 29. Residents were asked to bring any turtles they found to the Cranford Fire Department for safe transport to licensed rehabilitators. The Mercer County Wildlife Center now reports caring for 219 turtles connected to the July dumping, up from about 190 in early August. With colder weather approaching, the centre is building two outdoor enclosures where many of the turtles will be able to spend the winter following the same seasonal cycle.

Article Title: In 2011, California completed a 300-acre restoration of former San Diego salt ponds; five-year monitoring later documented 80 bird, 22 fish and 10 invertebrate species
Article Text:
Bringing the tides back

Wildlife began returning

A wetland begins to rebuild itself

From salt ponds to living wetlands

Poll Vote & Share your view Which aspect of the South San Diego Bay restoration do you find most impressive? Return of animal species Development of native plant communities Improvement in overall ecosystem health Creation of public observation areas 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

For decades, parts of South San Diego Bay looked very different from the tidal wetlands that once occupied them. Former salt ponds had been separated from the bay, limiting natural tidal flows and reducing habitat for wildlife. According to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the Southern California Wetlands Recovery Project, a partnership involving federal, state and local agencies and conservation groups began restoring the landscape in the late 2000s. By 2011, roughly 300 acres across the western salt ponds, the Chula Vista Wildlife Reserve and Emory Cove had been restored. The work included reshaping degraded areas, creating tidal channels, breaching levees to restore tidal influence and establishing native plant communities.Some of the western salt ponds had been cut off from tidal influence since around 1960 or earlier. During restoration, sediment was moved to create a network of channels and the existing levees were breached, allowing water from the bay and the Otay River channel to flow into the restored areas.The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service says the project ultimately transformed the former salt ponds into a combination of open water, intertidal habitat and upland marsh.The restoration was completed in 2011, with planting, maintenance and ecological monitoring continuing for five years afterward. The result was not simply a wetter landscape. It became habitat.The most striking evidence came from the post-construction monitoring programme. Over five years, researchers documented 80 species of birds, 22 species of fish and 10 species of invertebrates using the restored site.Birds were among the most visible beneficiaries. The restored wetlands provided feeding and foraging areas for migratory and resident species, while newly established marsh vegetation created habitat for species of conservation concern.The Southern California Wetlands Recovery Project says more than 90 species of migratory and residential birds are currently benefiting from the broader restoration area. Among them are the California least tern, light-footed Ridgway’s rail, western snowy plover and Belding’s savannah sparrow. The return of fish was equally significant. Reconnected tidal channels created shallow-water areas that could serve as feeding and spawning habitat, strengthening the ecological value of the bay.One of the clearest signs of recovery came surprisingly quickly. Native plants began appearing within less than a year of the restoration, according to the Fish and Wildlife Service.Researchers also found that the restored site was developing into nursery habitat for fish and invertebrates. Monitoring conducted after construction found natural recruitment of native vegetation, including eelgrass, which is an important food source for eastern Pacific green sea turtles. The project also helped create habitat for the endangered light-footed Ridgway’s rail, one of the restoration effort’s key targets. By 2016, the Fish and Wildlife Service reported successful breeding at the restored site.The restoration was part of a wider effort to recover coastal habitats that had been heavily altered by development, dredging and filling around San Diego Bay. Historical losses had left only a fraction of the bay’s original intertidal and salt-marsh habitat intact.Today, the restored landscape also offers people a chance to see the ecological changes firsthand through the Bayside Birding and Walking Trail, where visitors can observe birds using the marsh.What was once a landscape dominated by former industrial salt ponds has consequently become a functioning piece of the coastal ecosystem again. And the five-year monitoring results provide a measurable record of that change: 80 bird species, 22 fish species and 10 invertebrate species using habitat that had once been largely cut off from the tides.
Article Summary: The Southern California Wetlands Recovery Project restored 300 acres of salt ponds in South San Diego Bay. The restoration was completed in 2011, with planting, maintenance and ecological monitoring continuing for five years afterward. Researchers documented 80 species of birds, 22 species of fish and 10 species of invertebrates using the restored site.

Article Title: Third-generation Massachusetts farmer grows broccoli and sweet corn beneath 832 solar panels; his 2.2-acre agrivoltaic farm wins Farmer of the Year
Article Text:
Representative Image of a lush farm scene with solar panels overhead, showcasing broccoli and sweet corn growing below (AI Generated Image)

Massachusetts agrivoltaics farm: how Czajkowski Farm in Hadley hosts 832 solar panels over cropland

Crops under solar panels: broccoli and sweet corn grow beneath the array

Dual-use solar for farmers: how the array provides another source of farm income

On a stretch of farmland in Hadley, Massachusetts, broccoli, sweet corn and other crops have been grown beneath rows of solar panels. Farmer Joe Czajkowski, whose family has farmed in the Pioneer Valley for three generations, hosts an 832-panel agrivoltaic array covering 2.2 acres of his more than 400-acre farm. The 445-kilowatt DC system was built by Hyperion Systems and completed in July 2023, although the array became operational in 2024. The North American Agrivoltaics Awards has named Czajkowski its 2026 Solar Farmer of the Year, with the awards ceremony scheduled for October 27 in Chicago. The awards say half the electricity generated by the array runs his farm operations, while the other half goes to 17 low-income households across western Massachusetts. The U.S. Department of Energy says the panels are mounted at a 10-foot elevation to allow enough sunlight to reach crops below. UMass research and project materials from Hyperion describe the tracking system and its changing clearance above the ground.Czajkowski Farm covers more than 400 acres in the Pioneer Valley, and the 2.2-acre solar array occupies a small portion of that land. The project was developed through a partnership between Czajkowski and Hyperion Systems, a company specialising in dual-use solar.Hyperion's project information says the array has a capacity of 445 kilowatts DC and 375 kilowatts AC and consists of 832 modules mounted on single-axis trackers. The rows are spaced 26 feet from post to post, allowing farm equipment to operate between them. Czajkowski can continue using tractors and attachments for activities including subsoiling, tilling, harrowing, cultivating and spraying. The modules are 10 feet above the ground when horizontal, according to Hyperion. Because the system tracks the sun, the clearance changes as the panels tilt. The UMass research summary records a maximum tilt that brings the panels to about 7.75 feet above the ground. The array uses a north-south single-axis tracking system, with the modules following the sun from east to west. The UMass research records the system as completed in July 2023.The project was designed around the farm's existing agricultural operation. Czajkowski continues to prepare the soil, plant, cultivate and harvest crops beneath the array, while also using the land for a winter cover crop. The North American Agrivoltaics Awards says the project qualified for both the Massachusetts SMART Program's Low Income Community Solar standards and its Agricultural Solar Tariff Generation Unit standards. Half of the electricity generated goes toward the farm's operations, while the other half serves 17 low-income households in western Massachusetts.Broccoli was selected for a 2023 experiment examining how the agrivoltaic array affected the crop's growing conditions. The UMass research summary, titled Broccoli Production Under Agrivoltaic Solar Array in Hadley, MA, describes the work as first-year preliminary results. Researchers transplanted broccoli on August 18, 2023, and monitored three bed positions beneath the array: one under the leading panel, one between two panels and one near the back panel. They compared these positions with control plots. The study examined growing conditions and crop performance at the different positions beneath the array. The researchers found that the leading-panel position received less photosynthetically active radiation than the control, while the other two positions received similar light levels to the control. Air temperature, relative humidity and soil temperature were similar between the array and control areas. The researchers described the findings as a snapshot of how the panels modified the crop-level microclimate and said further time-series analysis was planned. One important detail is that the 2023 trial took place before the system was connected to the grid. The UMass report says the panels remained horizontal during that trial year, so those results describe the conditions during that specific experiment rather than the fully operational tracking configuration.The project has since expanded beyond broccoli. The 2026 North American Agrivoltaics Awards says Czajkowski has grown sweet corn, blueberries and shade tobacco beneath the panels and has also raised broiler chickens under the array. It says sweet corn grown beneath the panels is producing about 80% of the volume of open-field corn while maintaining matching quality. The awards page separately attributes the roughly 20% difference to fewer corn rows being planted rather than stunted growth. That result comes from this farm and should not be treated as a general yield figure for sweet corn grown under agrivoltaic systems elsewhere. The farm also supplies produce to institutional and retail customers, including UMass Amherst Dining Services, Springfield Public Schools, Trader Joe's and Whole Foods, according to Hyperion's project information. The North American Agrivoltaics Awards says an electric van charged from the array is used to transport produce to UMass Dining.For Czajkowski, reducing the farm's electricity costs was one reason he became interested in solar. American Farmland Trust reported that his average annual electricity bill was around $75,000 and that he became interested in solar as a way to decrease that cost. The organisation reported that, under the arrangement described in its November 2023 article, Czajkowski would receive a 17.5% discount on his monthly electricity bills as a subscriber, equivalent to about $13,125 a year based on the $75,000 annual bill. American Farmland Trust also reported that the parcel used for the project had previously grown almost exclusively onions and had experienced degraded soil. Czajkowski wanted to make the land more viable, while the agrivoltaic project provided another use for the acreage alongside continued agricultural production. The Department of Energy quoted him saying he receives payments for the electricity while also getting a discount on his electric bill. The exact lease-payment amount has not been publicly disclosed in the cited accounts. The percentage discount has been reported differently in different accounts. American Farmland Trust's November 2023 article described a 17.5% discount for the subscriber arrangement, while later reporting has cited a figure of about 15%. The reports do not explain the difference between the two figures.Czajkowski told the Department of Energy that the solar income could provide another layer of financial security as he gets older. He also discussed additional agrivoltaic projects as a way of helping keep the farm viable for the next generation. The Hadley project is part of a wider expansion of agrivoltaics in the United States. The National Renewable Energy Laboratory identified 566 U.S. agrivoltaic projects as of August 2024, with more than 10 gigawatts of combined capacity. The figure comes from research published when the laboratory was still known as the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL), now the National Laboratory of the Rockies. The U.S. Department of Energy's Solar Futures Study projected that solar could require about 5.7 million acres of land by 2035, equivalent to roughly 0.3% of the contiguous United States. DOE has highlighted agrivoltaics as one approach to combining solar generation with continued agricultural use of land. Its research and funding programmes have also examined how solar installations can coexist with crops and livestock.
Article Summary: Czajkowski Farm in Hadley hosts an 832-panel agrivoltaic array covering 2.2 acres of his more than 400-acre farm. The 445-kilowatt DC system was built by Hyperion Systems and completed in July 2023, although the array became operational in 2024. Half the electricity generated by the array runs his farm operations, while the other half goes to 17 low-income households across western Massachusetts.

Article Title: New York declares disaster emergency over measles, 108 cases reported
Article Text:
File Photo - A nurse, prepares a combination measles, mumps and rubella vaccine for a patient

108 cases reported in New York

US measles cases continue to climb

State expands vaccination efforts

New York state has declared a disaster emergency over a rise in measles cases, as the disease continues to spread across parts of the United States.Governor Kathy Hochul said the emergency declaration would expand the pool of health professionals who can administer measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccines and allow more healthcare workers to order testing.The declaration will remain in effect through November 4.New York has recorded 108 measles cases this year as of October 3, including seven in New York City and 101 elsewhere in the state.Hochul said 92 of the cases recorded since July 15 were in under-immunised rural communities across 18 counties.Local health departments have administered more than 1,000 MMR vaccine doses across rural parts of the state since July 15, according to the state health department.“No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease,” Hochul said, adding that the emergency measures would help increase access to vaccination and testing.The executive order allows paramedics, advanced EMS providers, pharmacists and midwives to administer measles vaccines. Nurses will also be allowed to order testing.The emergency declaration comes as measles cases rise across the US.Pennsylvania has reported more than 1,000 cases this year, while outbreaks have also been recorded in Texas, Utah, Ohio and South Carolina.Health experts have linked the resurgence to vaccination rates falling below the 95% level considered necessary to prevent outbreaks.The US had eliminated domestic transmission of measles in 2000. The last outbreak involving more than 1,000 cases occurred over several years in New York City in the early 1990s.International health officials are due to meet in November to determine whether the US and Mexico will retain their measles-free status.The Pan American Health Organisation has stressed the need for high and consistent vaccination coverage, stronger disease surveillance and a rapid response to outbreaks.New York's health department said it was working with local authorities to track cases, conduct contact tracing and speed up laboratory testing.The state has also launched a measles dashboard to help residents and healthcare officials track local risks.The health department urged New Yorkers to check their MMR vaccination status, particularly before travelling to areas experiencing outbreaks.It said one MMR dose provides 93% protection against measles, while two doses provide 97% protection.Measles is highly contagious and can cause serious complications including pneumonia, brain swelling and death. The disease spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes.The state health department urged people who develop symptoms to contact healthcare providers before visiting a clinic or hospital so that infection-control measures can be taken.
Article Summary: New York has recorded 108 measles cases this year as of October 3, including seven in New York City and 101 elsewhere in the state. 92 of the cases recorded since July 15 were in under-immunised rural communities across 18 counties. Emergency declaration will remain in effect through November 4.

Article Title: 'Expel rapists': Cornell students stage anti-rape rally in support of 'Jane Doe'
Article Text:
'Support survivors,' Cornell students rally for ‘Jane Doe'

Hundreds of Cornell University students, faculty members and community activists marched across the campus on Tuesday in support of a student known as “Jane Doe”, demanding greater accountability from the Ivy League university over its handling of her alleged gang rape.The protesters called for an independent inquiry into Cornell’s response, uniform minimum sanctions for sexual assault cases, independent hearings and better training for campus police. Some also demanded the resignation of university president Michael Kotlikoff and other administrators.Carrying purple ribbons and placards reading “support survivors, expel rapists” and “Justice 4 every Jane Doe”, demonstrators chanted “One struggle, one fight” and “No justice, no peace” as they marched to Cornell’s main administration building.“Too often, we are met with silence, we are met with statements, we are met with procedures, but not enough support,” news agency AP quoted student Athena Holloway saying. “How much does it take for our university to stand with survivors?”Hispanic studies professor Julia Chang told demonstrators: “Rape should not be inevitable.”The protest followed a lawsuit filed last month by Jane Doe, who alleged that she was drugged and sexually assaulted by several members of the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024 after becoming incapacitated.She named seven fraternity members, the fraternity chapter, a bar, her sorority and Cornell as defendants.Doe reported the alleged assault to Cornell police in November 2024. No criminal charges were filed at the time, though Cornell conducted its own investigation and later shut down the Chi Phi chapter. The university has said some students were expelled and others received suspensions or other disciplinary measures.The accused men have denied wrongdoing, with some telling Cornell investigators that the sexual activity was consensual, according to records cited by news organisations. Lawyers for two of the former students have denied that their clients participated in a sexual assault.The case has drawn renewed scrutiny after New York Governor Kathy Hochul appointed state Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to take over a reopened criminal investigation. Hochul has also called for an independent review of Cornell’s handling of the case.The university's administration has defended its response while acknowledging concerns raised by the allegations. In a video message on Saturday, Kotlikoff said Jane Doe's account “raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization and aspects of party culture, alcohol and drug use.”He also reaffirmed support for an independent review and pledged to work towards “finding the answers our community deserves.”The rally came after Cornell’s administration building was damaged early Monday, with two glass panes broken and graffiti painted on the entryway. One message read, “AT CORNELL RAPISTS ARE PROTECTED,” news agency Reuters reported.Cornell spokesperson Kyle Kimball said the university was investigating the damage, adding that “damaging property is not the answer” to the community's “frustration and strong emotions.”The controversy has also intensified online, with supporters using the hashtag #IamJaneDoe.ABC News reported Monday that Doe had recorded a phone call with one of the men she accused before approaching Cornell police. During the call, she challenged him over what she said had happened, telling him, “What y'all did would be classified as gang rape.”The investigation into the allegations remains ongoing.
Article Summary: Hundreds of Cornell University students, faculty members and community activists marched across the campus on Tuesday in support of a student known as ‘Jane Doe’ Protesters called for an independent inquiry into Cornell’s response, uniform minimum sanctions for sexual assault cases, independent hearings and better training for campus police.

Article Title: Another showdown brewing in Pakistan? Imran Khan supporters hit streets after talks fail
Article Text:
Supporters of imprisoned Imran Khan march towards Islamabad demanding his release.

Talks between PTI, government fail

Poll Vote & Share your view How do you feel about the government response to the PTI protests? It's appropriate and necessary. It's excessive and unjustified. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Thousands of supporters of jailed former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan began a march towards Islamabad on Sunday, demanding his release after talks between his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party and the government failed to break the political deadlock.Khan, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif's main political rival, has been in prison since 2023 on corruption and other charges. Khan and his party have described the cases as politically motivated, the Associated Press reported.Despite his imprisonment, he continues to command a large and committed support base.The protesters set off from Lakki Marwat district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where PTI is in power, in a convoy of trucks, buses and cars. Organisers have planned overnight stops as the caravan makes its way towards Islamabad.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister Sohail Afridi, a staunch Khan supporter, is leading the march. Speaking from a specially designed container truck bearing a large portrait of Khan, Afridi expressed confidence that the movement would succeed in taking its demands to the heart of the capital.Authorities have erected roadblocks using shipping containers at entry points to Islamabad and at several locations inside the city.PTI and the federal government had held talks over postponing the march, but failed to reach an agreement. PTI chairman Gohar Khan said negotiations remained deadlocked after two rounds.Interior minister Mohsin Naqvi blamed Afridi for the failure of the talks and warned that he would be held responsible for any loss of life during the planned march.The government had urged PTI to postpone the protest, citing a rise in militant attacks by the Pakistani Taliban, also known as Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), in the northwest. The government has also accused PTI of sympathising with the TTP.PTI organisers, however, have vowed to reach Islamabad after mobilising hundreds of thousands of Khan supporters. Apart from Khan's release, protesters are demanding that he be shifted to a hospital and that his family be allowed to visit him.Officials have said Khan is in good health and receives regular family visits, but maintain that meetings with the imprisoned former prime minister cannot be used for political purposes.The march was originally scheduled for September 27 but was postponed after PTI leaders said authorities had blocked key routes to Islamabad, including the Attock Bridge, a major crossing used by convoys from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.Previous protests by Khan's supporters have turned violent. During one such protest in 2024, security personnel and civilians were killed.
Article Summary: Talks between PTI, government fail to break political deadlock. Protesters set off from Lakki Marwat district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where PTI is in power, in a convoy of trucks, buses and cars. Khan has been in prison since 2023 on corruption and other charges.

Article Title: Pakistan braces for showdown as talks collapse, Imran Khan’s party pushes ahead with march
Article Text:
Imran Khan has been incarcerated since 2023.

PTI demands access to Imran Khan

Government and PTI blame each other

Long march to begin from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa

Poll Vote & Share your view Should the federal government negotiate further with PTI? Yes, dialogue is essential No, they should stand firm Only under certain conditions 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan’s opposition Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party will proceed with its planned long march towards Islamabad after a second round of talks with the government ended without a deal on access to jailed former prime minister Imran Khan The negotiations began at 4 pm on Saturday and continued into the early hours of Sunday, but the two sides failed to resolve their differences. The main dispute centred on PTI’s demand for an immediate meeting with Khan, including access to his personal doctor.PTI had initially planned to start the long march on September 27 but postponed it to October 4 after the federal government introduced measures aimed at preventing the protest.The party wants an immediate meeting with Khan and has demanded that he be taken to a hospital where his personal doctors can examine him.Khan, 73, has been in jail since 2023 after being convicted in a corruption case. He is currently held at the high-security Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi.PTI has also called for the release of Khan’s sisters and other people arrested ahead of the protest. It wants a proper medical examination of Khan’s wife, Bushra Bibi, and has demanded that their legal cases be heard without interference.The government, however, insisted that PTI first cancel the protest before it would consider allowing its leaders to meet Khan, according to sources. PTI rejected that condition and wanted access to its jailed leader before deciding whether to call off the march.Tehreek-e-Tahafuz-e-Ayin-e-Pakistan leader Senator Allama Nasir Abbas said the negotiations had failed because the two sides could not agree on the roles of the federal and provincial governments in dealing with terrorism in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, as well as access to Khan.“No understanding could be reached regarding the respective roles of the province and the federal government concerning terrorism in the province, and the matter of a meeting with Imran Khan remains unresolved,” Abbas, who is also Leader of the Opposition in the Senate, said.“We endeavoured to reach a conclusion, but the deadlock persists -- specifically regarding access to Khan Sahib's personal physician,” he added.Minister of State for Interior Tallal Chaudhry said the talks failed mainly because the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government could not guarantee that it would cooperate with the federal government in the fight against terrorism in the future.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa is governed by PTI, and the province is also where the planned march will begin.Pakistan Peoples Party leader Sherry Rehman, who took part in the negotiations, said the government delegation had discussed all the opposition's demands.“Unfortunately, the draft [agreement] was changed four times after it was agreed upon,” she told Geo News, adding that she would not go into the details.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi announced at 12:46 am that the protest would go ahead.He said supporters from Tank, Dera Ismail Khan, South Waziristan, North Waziristan, Bannu and Lakki Marwat would join the march at Gandi Chowk in Lakki Marwat at 1 pm on Sunday.The convoy is scheduled to stop near Karak for the night before leaving at 12:30 pm the following day and staying overnight near Kohat.On October 6, protesters from Kohat, Hangu, Kurram and Orakzai will join the convoy as it moves towards Peshawar, with the group expected to spend the night near Mattani.Afridi said the caravan would leave Budh Bair in Peshawar on the afternoon of October 7. Supporters from other parts of Peshawar will join at Kohat Road Bridge and the Motorway Toll Plaza before the convoy moves towards Charsadda.“The remaining constituencies of Peshawar will join us at Kohat Road Bridge and the Motorway Toll Plaza. And we will spend the night near Charsadda Interchange,” he said.The protesters are scheduled to leave Charsadda Interchange at 12:30 pm on October 8 after supporters from Charsadda and Mohmand join them.Afridi said people from across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa would gather at Khairabad later that day before the next stage of the march is announced.“God willing, the plan for the next phase will be announced there,” he said.The federal government has warned that the protesters will not be allowed to enter Islamabad. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif ’s political adviser Rana Sanaullah said authorities would prevent the march from reaching the capital.“No one would be allowed to enter Islamabad,” he told reporters.The government had earlier said it would block roads leading into Islamabad with shipping containers and deploy additional security personnel to prevent the protesters from entering the capital.
Article Summary: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party will proceed with its planned long march towards Islamabad. The party wants an immediate meeting with Khan and has demanded that he be taken to a hospital where his personal doctors can examine him. The government, however, insisted that PTI first cancel the protest before it would consider allowing its leaders to meet Khan.

Article Title: India slams Pakistan at UN, says ‘so-called’ civilian governments serve at army’s mercy
Article Text:
Pakistan's Prime Minister Muhammad Shehbaz Sharif

India on Friday hit back at Pakistan at the UN General Assembly, rejecting Islamabad’s remarks on Jammu and Kashmir and accusing its “so-called” civilian governments of serving “at the mercy” of the army.Exercising its Right of Reply during a Third Committee meeting, first secretary at the Permanent Mission of India to the UN Bhavika Mangalanandan said Pakistan’s civilian governments “rarely complete their terms”, while accusing Islamabad of using cross-border terrorism to divert attention from domestic discontent.Accoridng to news agency PTI, India “categorically” rejected Pakistan’s remarks on Jammu and Kashmir, asserting that the Union Territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh were, are and will always remain “integral and inalienable” parts of India.“We all know that the so-called civilian governments in Pakistan serve at the mercy of their army and rarely complete their terms,” Mangalanandan said.Referring to jailed former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan, she said a “former Prime Minister continues to remain in jail, even as his health is reported to be fast deteriorating.”She also said the erstwhile ruling party had not been allowed to contest elections.“Instead of addressing domestic discontent, Pakistan seeks to distract by fomenting instability in India and sponsoring, inciting, abetting, and financing cross-border terrorism in my country for more than three decades,” she said.Turning to Jammu and Kashmir, Mangalanandan said, “The only outstanding matter is a vacation of the territory Pakistan holds under illegal and forcible occupation.She accused Pakistan of attempting to divert attention from unrest in the country.“This is a desperate attempt by Pakistan to mask the ongoing tragedy in Rawalakot and its other cities, the killing of hundreds of civilians, and the brutal crackdown across Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir, for merely demanding bread, electricity and human dignity,” she said.India also invoked the term “Form 47”, used in reference to allegations of rigging and manipulation in Pakistan’s 2024 general elections.“When any free media is banned from covering such news in Pakistan, the evidence becomes undeniable for the global community that only the writ of the Form 47 government and their masters and the army headquarters runs large,” she said.Contrasting this with Jammu and Kashmir, India said Assembly Elections were held there in 2024, followed by a peaceful transfer of power to an elected government.“The contrast could not have been starker. The only human rights violation taking place in Kashmir is perpetrated by the armed forces of Pakistan and their terrorist proxies. Propaganda does not become fact through repetition,” Mangalanandan said.“Pakistan would serve its people better by confronting its own fault lines and building its economy than by coveting the territory of others,” she added.
Article Summary: India “categorically” rejected Pakistan’s remarks on Jammu and Kashmir, asserting that the Union Territories of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh were, are and will always remain “integral and inalienable”

Article Title: Pakistan kills 5 TTP militants as violence escalates on Afghanistan border
Article Text:
The militants reportedly belonged to Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, which the government calls Fitna al-Khawarij (Representative image: Reuters).

Pakistani security forces killed five militants during an intelligence-based operation on Saturday in the country's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.The militants reportedly belonged to Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan , which the government calls Fitna al-Khawarij.The operation was carried out in KPK's South Waziristan district, based on intelligence about several militant hideouts, PTI reported, citing an official.A large quantity of weapons and ammunition was also recovered, the official said.Pak army has been targeting such hideouts amid increased violence at the Afghanistan border.On Friday, seven militants belonging to the same group were killed in North Waziristan district. Such operations form part of Pakistan's Azm-e-Istehkam initiative, aimed at countering terrorism.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has long struggled with instability, fueled by militant violence, the movement of fighters across the border from Afghanistan, and repeated military campaigns.After its ceasefire agreement with the Pakistani government collapsed in November 2022, the TTP has launched a series of attacks in the province, which borders Afghanistan.Last week, a suicide bombing at a roadside police checkpoint in KPK's Dera Ismail Khan district killed more than a dozen security personnel and wounded at least 30 others. Nearly 21 people died in the city of Kohat after a car loaded with explosives rammed into the entrance of a mosque; both attacks were linked to the TTP.According to the Centre for Research and Security Studies, an Islamabad-based think tank, KPK was Pakistan's worst-hit region for violence in the third quarter of 2025. The region recorded around 638 violence-related deaths, nearly 71 per cent of the national total. KPK also faced 221 violent incidents, more than 67 per cent of the total.Overall, Pakistan recorded 1,232 rebel group attacks during the first nine months of 2026, according to a report by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies, with the number of attacks in September reaching a 12-year high.
Article Summary: Militants reportedly belonged to Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, which the government calls Fitna al-Khawarij. Operation carried out in KPK's South Waziristan district, based on intelligence about several militant hideouts. A large quantity of weapons and ammunition was also recovered.

Article Title: Pakistan logs over 1.2k rebel attacks in 9 months of ’26, security crisis deepens
Article Text: During the first nine months of 2026, Pakistan recorded 1,232 rebel group attacks, according to a report by Islamabad-based think tank Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies, indicating that a major security crisis is brewing. The number of attacks in Sept reached a 12-year high, with 225 attacks resulting in 545 deaths. Police and military personnel have been the primary targets of these operations, accounting for majority of fatalities.Spearheaded by groups such as Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), Baloch Liberation Army, Baloch Liberation Front and alliances like Ittehad Mujahideen Pakistan, these attacks remain concentrated in Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and former tribal areas. Formed in 2025, IMP is the latest threat and comprises three sub-outfits — Hafiz Gul Bahadur group (HGBG), Lashkar-e-Islam and Harakat Inqilab-e-Islami Pakistan.Just last week, over a dozen security personnel were killed and at least 30 wounded in a suicide bombing at a roadside police checkpoint in Dera Ismail Khan district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. A week before that around 21 Pakistani security personnel were killed and dozens injured in a powerful suicide bombing and subsequent firing at the police line and intelligence facility in Kohat, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.The surge in Sept represents a 13% increase from 199 incidents reported in Aug, marking the third consecutive month of compounding violence.Balochistan served as the primary epicentre of the escalation, bearing the brunt of the violence with 131 recorded attacks, accounting for more than half of all nationwide incidents. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa followed with 58 attacks, while the former tribal areas recorded 34 incidents, the institute claimed. Tensions between Islamabad and Kabul have risen as Pakistan repeatedly accuses the ruling Afghan Taliban of providing safe havens and operational freedom to the TTP.
Article Summary: During the first nine months of 2026, Pakistan recorded 1,232 rebel group attacks. The number of attacks in Sept reached a 12-year high, with 225 attacks resulting in 545 deaths. Police and military personnel have been the primary targets of these operations.

Article Title: Shehbaz govt, Imran Khan’s PTI hold talks as Pakistan braces for protests
Article Text: Pakistan’s federal government and jailed former prime minister Imran Khan ’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) agreed to hold a second round of talks on Saturday, as the opposition party prepares for a long march towards Islamabad from October 4.The first round of negotiations was held on Friday in the chamber of national assembly speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq, who is facilitating the dialogue amid heightened security in the capital.According to a statement issued by the National Assembly Secretariat, the participants held detailed discussions “on the prevailing political situation and exchanged views on various matters of national importance”.“The government, PPP and opposition representatives apprised each other of their respective positions and held a detailed exchange of views constructively and cordially. The participants emphasised the need to resolve national issues through dialogue and negotiations,” it said, according to news agency PTI.The second round will be held at 2 pm on Saturday in the speaker’s chamber.Sadiq said he was “only playing the role of a mediator”, adding that his office was “always open” to resolving issues through negotiations.“Parliament is the only forum where solutions to issues can be found,” he said, stressing that negotiations were the way to address political differences.PTI international spokesman Zulfiqar Bukhari said the talks were “primarily aimed at defusing the current political situation surrounding PTI’s planned march/protest toward Islamabad on October 4”.Bukhari said the party’s demands included an “immediate” meeting with Khan and a decision to take him to hospital so his personal doctors could examine him. PTI has also sought the release of Khan’s sisters and others arrested ahead of the protest, a medical check-up for his wife Bushra Bibi and proper hearings in their cases.Meanwhile, the Pakistan authorities have deployed additional police and placed shipping containers on routes into Islamabad. The blockades have already disrupted freight movement.Bukhari said the long march would begin from Gandi Chowk in Lakki Marwat, with stops planned in Karak and Kohat on October 5 before entering Peshawar district.
Article Summary: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf to hold second round of talks on Saturday. Opposition party preparing for long march towards Islamabad from October 4. First round of negotiations was held on Friday in the chamber of national assembly speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq.

Article Title: 'Vague and broad': UN experts slam Pakistan's counter-terrorism laws, demand release of lawyer couple
Article Text:
UN experts demand release of Pakistani lawyers, question terror laws

United Nations human rights experts have stepped up pressure on Pakistan to release Pakistani lawyers Imaan Mazari-Hazir and Hadi Ali Chattha, after the married couple was rearrested on terrorism-related charges just hours after the Supreme Court granted them bail on September 17.The Office of the UN high commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) said that the latest charges relate to an earlier case dating back to March 2025, when the two lawyers were accused in connection with their participation in a protest that authorities deemed illegal.The UN experts said they had already expressed concern over the couple’s conviction in a separate case involving social media posts in which they supported local activists and criticised the military.They said the decision to invoke an older case immediately after Mazari-Hazir and Chattha secured bail “appears to be an attempt” to use the criminal justice system to punish freedom of expression and human rights advocacy.The couple’s rearrest was followed by proceedings before an Islamabad anti-terrorism court. Police had sought 30 days of custody for interrogation, but the court rejected the request and ordered that the lawyers be sent to jail on a 14-day judicial remand, OHCHR said.Their legal proceedings continued on September 22, when an Islamabad anti-terrorism court returned their bail petitions because they did not carry signed powers of attorney, according to the UN rights office.The UN experts also raised broader concerns about Pakistan’s use of counter-terrorism legislation, criticising what they described as “vague and broad” provisions that could be used to restrict human rights and interfere with legitimate advocacy.They called on Pakistani authorities to drop any charges stemming from the lawyers’ exercise of freedom of expression or their legitimate professional work.The experts also urged authorities to ensure that the couple had access to lawyers of their choice, their families and necessary medical care.The UN experts said they had been in contact with the Pakistani government over their concerns.
Article Summary: Pakistani lawyers Imaan Mazari-Hazir and Hadi Ali Chattha were rearrested on terrorism-related charges just hours after the Supreme Court granted them bail. The UN experts said they had already expressed concern over the couple’s conviction in a separate case involving social media posts in which they supported local activists.

Article Title: Policeman killed in gunmen attack in Pakistan’s khyber pakhtunkhwa
Article Text:
A police officer was killed in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

A police officer was killed in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province after two armed med riding a motorcycle attacked him with a hand grenede and fired at him while he was deployed outside a hospital, police said.The attack took place in the unstable province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's Tank area.The banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) later claimed the responsibility for the attack, as per the PTI report.According to the police, the two attackers escaped from the spot on their motorcyclen after the attackSecurity personnel have launched a search operation to trace the assailants, while an investigation into the incident is also in progress.Over the years, there have been several instances of terrorist violence in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which shares a border with Afghanistan. The transfer of combatants across borders and subsequent military actions have also been connected to the disturbance.The TTP has continued to carry out attacks in the province since its ceasefire agreement with the Pakistani government ended in November
Article Summary: The attack took place in the unstable province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's Tank area. The banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) later claimed responsibility for the attack. The TTP has continued to carry out attacks in the province since its ceasefire agreement with the Pakistani government ended in November.

Article Title: Pakistan forces kill 7 TTP militants in North Waziristan amid rising violence along Afghan border
Article Text:
Pakistan military-led government refers to the banned TTP as Fitna al Khawarij.

Seven militants belonging to the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) were killed by security forces during an intelligence-based operation in north-western Pakistan on Friday, according to an official.The operation took place in Eidak, an area of North Waziristan district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, which has witnessed repeated militant attacks in recent years.Security forces also destroyed several hideouts during the operation, the official said. The action was carried out under the government's Azm-e-Istehkam move, which is part of Pakistan's purported efforts to tackle terrorism.Pakistan's federal government refers to the banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, or TTP, as Fitna al Khawarij.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has remained a major hotspot for militant violence, partly because of its border with Afghanistan. The region has also seen repeated military operations and the movement of fighters across the border.The TTP ended its ceasefire with the Pakistani military-led government in November 2022. Since then, the group has carried out repeated attacks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, particularly against security forces.Figures from the Centre for Research and Security Studies show that Khyber Pakhtunkhwa was Pakistan's worst-hit region for violence in the third quarter of 2025.It recorded 638 violence-related deaths, accounting for nearly 71 per cent of the national total, along with 221 violent incidents, or more than 67 per cent of the total.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, both of which border Afghanistan, together accounted for more than 96 per cent of militant-related violence recorded in Pakistan during that period.Separately, Reuters sources reported an attack on a convoy of paramilitary troops in the volatile Kurram district. Roadside bombs struck the convoy before a large group of militants opened fire, according to five Pakistani security officials.The Pakistani Taliban claimed responsibility for that attack in a statement to a Reuters reporter. Pakistan's military public relations wing did not immediately respond to requests for comment.Security forces launched a search operation to locate those responsible, while the government had not issued an official statement at the time of the report.The TTP has intensified attacks on Pakistani security forces in recent months. The group seeks to overthrow the Pakistani government and establish its own hardline interpretation of Islamic rule.Islamabad has accused Afghanistan of allowing the TTP to use its territory to train fighters and plan attacks inside Pakistan. Kabul has denied the allegation.
Article Summary: Seven militants belonging to the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) were killed by security forces during an intelligence-based operation. The operation took place in Eidak, an area of North Waziristan district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province. Security forces also destroyed several hideouts during the operation, the official said.

Article Title: Jail, isolation, crackdown: Why Pakistan’s establishment has failed to break Imran Khan
Article Text:
Former Pakistan PM Imran Khan has been incarcerated since 2023 (File photo)

How Imran Khan got here

Why Imran Khan matters

Imran Khan: From cricket captain to PM to inmate

How state failed to marginalise Imran Khan politically

Imran Khan: PTI's 'red line'

The 'persecution' of Imran Khan

Main legal cases against Imran Khan

Imran Khan: A case that resonates beyond politics

The state’s struggle to marginalise Imran Khan

Islamabad had prepared for another confrontation. Roads were blocked, security forces deployed and Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) supporters were expected to march towards the capital demanding the release of their jailed leader, Imran Khan Then, days before the September 27 protest, PTI postponed the march until October 4, temporarily easing the pressure on the government.But the roads can be reopened and the barricades removed. The political problem surrounding Imran Khan is proving harder to clear.The former prime minister has now spent more than three years behind bars. The establishment has used imprisonment, restrictions on his contact with the outside world, scores of legal cases and a crackdown on his supporters. Yet none of it has so far succeeded in removing Imran Khan from the centre of Pakistan's politics. PTI-backed independents won the largest number of directly elected national assembly seats in the 2024 general election, and his supporters continue to mobilise around demands for his release.The postponed Islamabad march is therefore less an end to the latest confrontation than another pause in a political standoff that has survived elections, convictions and imprisonment.Imran Khan retired from international cricket in 1992, shortly after leading Pakistan to its first and, so far, only 50-over Cricket World Cup title. Four years later, in 1996, he formally entered politics by founding the PTI.His political breakthrough finally came after the 2018 general election, when the PTI emerged as the single-largest party and he became prime minister. His rise to power was widely seen by rivals and analysts as having benefited from the backing of Pakistan’s military, the country’s most powerful institution, although both Khan and the military denied that the army had helped bring him to power.That relationship subsequently deteriorated. In April 2022, the opposition brought a parliamentary no-confidence vote against Imran Khan, which he lost and was thus removed from office.He has since faced more than 100 cases, many involving corruption allegations. Several of his convictions have been overturned, suspended or otherwise challenged, while he has consistently denied wrongdoing.Imran Khan was imprisoned in August 2023 and has remained behind bars since then. Yet his incarceration has done little to diminish his presence in Pakistan’s public life or erase him from the public consciousness.Thanks to his cricket career, Imran Khan was already a well-known public figure before entering politics. Following his retirement, he gained further goodwill by giving Pakistan its first specialised cancer hospital, the Shaukat Khanum Memorial Cancer Hospital, named after his mother, in Lahore. The hospital opened in 1994.That personal following later became the foundation of a political movement, the PTI, that presented him as an outsider challenging Pakistan’s established political order. In a country where civilian politics has long been shaped by the Bhutto-Zardari and Sharif families, Imran Khan offered voters a figure outside the traditional political dynasties. His image as a retired cricket captain with no family legacy in politics helped distinguish him from the established political class.His prime ministership brought him further visibility and established him as a central figure in Pakistan’s civilian politics.And therein lies his significance: an outsider who challenged Pakistan’s established political dynasties, became prime minister, and later fell out with the military establishment before being jailed.Pakistan’s 2024 general election offered the clearest indication that Imran Khan’s imprisonment had not erased his political relevance. Despite the PTI being stripped of its election symbol and Imran Khan remaining in prison, PTI-backed independents won 92 directly elected National Assembly seats — more than candidates backed by any other political grouping.While that result did not bring the party back to power, it showed that his absence from the ballot did not translate into the disappearance of his support.However, the outcome should not have been a surprise. In October 2022, just months after his ouster as prime minister, Imran Khan contested by-elections in seven of eight National Assembly constituencies voting on October 16. He won six of the seven seats he contested, while the Pakistan People’s Party won the other two constituencies.He then won another by-election in Kurram on October 30, taking his tally of by-election victories that month to seven.The by-election results offered an early indication that removing Imran Khan from office had not dented his electoral support. The 2024 elections reinforced that point, showing that his imprisonment and the restrictions placed on the PTI had not eliminated its support among voters.As its founder and most prominent face, PTI has repeatedly described Imran Khan as its “red line.” The phrase took on greater significance after his arrest on May 9, 2023, when Pakistan witnessed widespread rioting and arson by PTI supporters. Protesters targeted government buildings and military installations, including the residence of a corps commander in Lahore and the army’s general headquarters in Rawalpindi.The events marked a dramatic escalation in the confrontation between Imran Khan and the military establishment. They also demonstrated why the PTI has continued to place him at the centre of its politics: attempts to remove him from the political arena have not removed the attachment to him among a significant section of the party’s supporters.Since his incarceration, the party has repeatedly mobilised in Islamabad, demanding his release. The federal government’s frustration with these protests was evident ahead of the recently postponed Islamabad march, when interior minister Mohsin Naqvi spoke of the need to find a “permanent solution” to the PTI’s repeated demonstrations in the capital.“This time we will find a permanent solution; we will not leave it halfway,” Naqvi said.Therefore, Imran Khan remains the PTI’s “red line” — one reason efforts to marginalise him politically have so far struggled to succeed.Imran Khan’s prolonged imprisonment has also strengthened a persecution narrative around him. His party and supporters have consistently argued that the numerous cases against him are politically motivated and intended to keep him out of politics. Pakistani authorities have rejected those allegations.The fact that more than 100 cases have been brought against him, his disqualification by the Election Commission in 2022, and the restrictions imposed on the PTI ahead of the 2024 general elections have only strengthened that narrative among his supporters.The conditions of his imprisonment at Rawalpindi’s Adiala Jail have added another dimension to the persecution narrative.In December 2025, UN Special Rapporteur on torture Alice Jill Edwards raised concerns over reports that Khan was being held in conditions falling below international standards for humane and dignified detention. The communication cited allegations of prolonged solitary confinement, restricted access to the outside world and inadequate ventilation.Edwards subsequently urged Pakistani authorities to end his reported solitary confinement and ensure that his detention conditions complied with international standards, warning that the reported conditions could amount to torture or other inhuman or degrading treatment.The Pakistani establishment has succeeded in keeping Imran Khan behind bars. But with so many eyes on his case, it has not succeeded in making his political relevance disappear.The controversy surrounding Imran Khan’s imprisonment has increasingly extended beyond politics and Pakistan, as his cricketing legacy has kept his case in the international spotlight.Former international cricket captains have appealed to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s government over Khan’s treatment and access to medical care. In August, 21 former captains urged the government to ensure “humane treatment and proper medical care” for their former on-field rival.Matters almost came to a head during the recent England-Pakistan Test series. During the second Test at Lord’s, the Pakistan Cricket Board reportedly considered not sending its players back onto the field after the lunch break after Sky Sports aired an interview with Imran Khan’s sons, Kasim and Suleiman.The PCB ultimately returned to the field and lodged a complaint with the broadcaster.The episode underscored how Imran Khan’s imprisonment continues to attract attention beyond Pakistan and outside politics.Every time the PTI has marched on Islamabad, the Pakistan government has responded by fortifying the capital, blocking entry routes and deploying thousands of police and paramilitary personnel.Ahead of the September 27 march, authorities deployed thousands of security personnel and erected extensive barricades and roadblocks around Islamabad.The crackdown extended to Imran Khan’s family too, with his three sisters detained ahead of the now-postponed march.Such measures may prevent protesters from reaching Islamabad, but they have not stopped the PTI from returning to the streets with the same central demand: Imran Khan’s release. The state has managed to contain individual protests, but each confrontation has been followed by another, keeping his imprisonment at the centre of Pakistan’s politics.By isolating him in prison and cracking down on his family and party, the Pakistani authorities have sought to contain Imran Khan’s political influence. So far, however, his electoral support, PTI’s continued mobilisation and the attention surrounding his imprisonment show that those measures have not removed him from the country’s political contest.For now, Imran Khan’s ability to retain political relevance despite his imprisonment remains a significant feature of Pakistan’s politics.
Article Summary: Former Pakistan PM Imran Khan has been incarcerated since 2023. He has faced more than 100 cases, many involving corruption allegations. Several of his convictions have been overturned, suspended or otherwise challenged. Yet none of it has so far succeeded in removing Imran Khan from the centre of Pakistan's politics.

Article Title: BLF’s newly-formed female unit 'KAAD' attacks military convoy in Balochistan; claims nine killed
Article Text:
Image credit: X

The Balochistan Liberation Front (BLF) has released footage of an attack by its newly formed female unit on a Pakistani military convoy in Turbat, claiming that nine security personnel were killed in the operation.The video, released through the group’s media cell Aashoob, shows fighters of the Karima Armed Assault Division (KAAD) firing at a three-vehicle Quick Response Force (QRF) convoy on the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) highway on September 22.The footage includes a female commander briefing fighters before the operation, along with training clips. It also shows the fighters opening fire on the convoy from close range. The group claimed that several military vehicles were severely damaged and that several personnel were injured. These claims could not be independently verified.BLF spokesperson Major Gwahram Baloch said the group’s Qurban unit supported the operation and helped its fighters resist an attempt by Pakistani forces to encircle them, while covering their withdrawal. He said Qurban unit fighter Chakar Murad, alias Dileep Jan, was killed during the attack.The video also shows KAAD members conducting snap checks of vehicles in the Mangchar area of Kalat. The BLF claimed that its fighters carried out a blockade and vehicle checks there.In a separate incident, the Baloch Republican Army (BRA) claimed responsibility for an attack on a Mari Energies Limited site in the Beh Loti area of Dera Bugti, using rockets and heavy weapons.BRA spokesperson Sarbaz Baloch claimed that three company employees were killed and several others injured. He said a clash followed between Pakistani forces and members of a local armed group. The BRA claimed nine Pakistani military personnel and three members of the armed group were killed, while six of its own fighters also lost their lives, according to The Balochistan Post.The Baloch Republican Guards (BRG) separately claimed that its fighters seized Haji Shehr and destroyed a local police station using explosives. It also said BRA fighters entered Eri Shehr, took control of government facilities and withdrew after the operation.KAAD is named after Karima Baloch, a pro-independence activist and the first woman chairperson of the Baloch Students Organisation-Azad. She was found dead in Toronto in 2020.
Article Summary: Balochistan Liberation Front (BLF) claims nine security personnel were killed in the operation. Video shows fighters of the Karima Armed Assault Division (KAAD) firing at a three-vehicle Quick Response Force (QRF) convoy on the China- Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) highway.

Article Title: 'Technical issue': Pakistan blocks airspace for Russian flight carrying uranium for Bangladesh nuclear plant
Article Text:
Russia’s uranium shipment for Bangladesh’s Rooppur nuclear plant delayed (Image credit: Reuters)

Poll Vote & Share your view Should international diplomatic norms allow for expedited clearance of flights carrying critical supplies like nuclear fuel? Definitely Not at all 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: Pakistan has denied airspace clearance to a Russian cargo flight carrying nuclear fuel for Bangladesh's Rooppur nuclear power plant, delaying the scheduled arrival of uranium for the facility's Unit 2. Pakistan later described the matter as a "technical and procedural" issue involving flight routing and airspace permissions.The nuclear fuel was scheduled to arrive in Bangladesh on September 24 but did not reach the country after the aircraft was not allowed to use Pakistani airspace. Russia has now proposed the first week of October as a new arrival date, according to Bangladesh officials as cited by news agency ANI."We heard that a cargo plane carrying uranium for the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant in Bangladesh was scheduled to arrive on September 24. However, the flight was not given permission to use Pakistani airspace, so the uranium did not arrive in Bangladesh as planned. As of now, the exact reason for Pakistan not granting the airspace clearance is still unknown", ANI quoted Bangladesh's minister for science and technology Faqir Mahbub Anam saying."A new date has been proposed, with Russia indicating the first week of October for the uranium to arrive in Bangladesh", he added.Sheikh Mohammed Tauhidul Islam, joint secretary in Bangladesh's science and technology ministry, said preparations had been completed at the airport before officials were informed that the airspace was unavailable."We had completed all the preparations at the airport and were waiting, but the liaison officer from Rosatom told us that the airspace was not clear. So we couldn’t send it. It may need to be rescheduled", he said.Pakistan's high commission in Dhaka, in a clarification, said the matter was related to technical and procedural arrangements."Pakistan maintains an unwavering commitment to international diplomatic norms and processes all requests for diplomatic flight and overflight clearances within a standardised, predictable timeframe, strictly in accordance with our established regulatory guidelines and civil aviation protocols," ANI quoted it as saying."With regard to the reports being quoted, the matter appears to relate to technical and procedural arrangements concerning flight routing and airspace permissions, which can occasionally require coordination among the relevant aviation and other authorities and may result in adjustments to flight schedules", it added.The high commission also said the incident should not be linked to Pakistan-Bangladesh ties."Pakistan attaches high importance to its relations with Bangladesh, and it would therefore be appropriate to view the matter in its proper technical context and not attach undue significance to reports or narratives that may seek to misplace it to undermine our bilateral relations," it said.The Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant, Bangladesh's first nuclear power facility, is being built with technical assistance from Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom. The project comprises two VVER-1200 reactor units with a combined capacity of 2,400 MW.
Article Summary: The nuclear fuel was scheduled to arrive in Bangladesh on September 24 but did not reach the country after the aircraft was not allowed to use Pakistani airspace. Pakistan later described the matter as a "technical and procedural" issue involving flight routing and airspace permissions. Russia has now proposed the first week of October as a new arrival date.

Article Title: 'Took mobile phones, cash': Karachi football team robbed at gunpoint on Balochistan highway
Article Text:
Image credit X @Baloch_Nojawan

NEW DELHI: A football team travelling from Karachi to Quetta to participate in the Chief Minister’s Gold Cup tournament was robbed at gunpoint on a highway in Pakistan’s Balochistan province, PTI reported on Monday.Around a dozen armed men intercepted the Karachi District West team’s bus between Mastung and Sariab, and took away the players’ mobile phones, cash and other valuables. The incident took place on Monday evening, leaving the players without money.Team manager Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto said the armed men ordered all passengers to get off the bus before robbing them."The armed men asked all the passengers to disembark from the bus and then took away all mobile phones, cash, and other valuables. They also butted some of the passengers."After reaching Quetta, the team informed Balochistan’s sports minister about the robbery. The minister intervened to provide the players with daily allowances, according to the report.Muhammad Azam, secretary of the Sindh Football Association, an affiliated unit of the Pakistan Football Federation, said the team had travelled despite official warnings against using road and rail routes to Quetta."We didn't send the Sindh team and we advised all other clubs in Karachi to avoid going to Quetta by bus or train because of the security situation. The Karachi west team still went ahead and what we feared happened," Muhammad Azam said.He added that the Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa football associations had also not sent teams for the tournament.The incident comes days after two local cricketers were abducted from Dera Bugti.The highway connecting Mastung district to Quetta has become a hotspot for armed groups targeting travellers, PTI reported.
Article Summary: A football team travelling from Karachi to Quetta was robbed at gunpoint. Around a dozen armed men intercepted the Karachi District West team’s bus. They took away the players’ mobile phones, cash and other valuables.

Article Title: Child, forced marriages of minority girls in Pakistan flagged at UN event
Article Text:
UN rights event highlights risks faced by girls in Pakistan’s child marriages (ANI photo)

The impact of child and forced marriages on girls in Pakistan, particularly those from minority communities, was discussed at a side event during the 63rd session of the United Nations Human Rights Council in Geneva.Speakers at the event raised concerns about girls being married at a young age and the consequences for their education, health and basic rights. The event was reported by Global Human Rights Defence, a UN ECOSOC-accredited human rights organisation.Naveed Walter, president of Human Rights Focus Pakistan and a human rights defender, pointed to the scale of child rights violations in Pakistan and the vulnerability of children who enter marriage at an early age.“Most recently, UNICEF gave the data about Pakistan. Ninety million women and children and girls have been affected by child rights violations. And of them, 4.8 million were under 15 years of age,” Walter said.Walter said early marriage can leave girls without access to basic education and expose them to serious health risks, particularly during pregnancy.“You know, dear excellencies and dear audience, that during pregnancy, millions of children have died.And you know, under 30 per cent of the children who get married even have basic education,” he said.The discussion also focused on Sindh, where women's rights activist Shagufta Kandhro highlighted the situation of girls who are married before reaching adulthood.“According to the National Commission on the Rights of the Child, 84,000 children between the ages of 10 and 17 are married, widowed and separated. Many of them have already left school, and many face serious health risks,” Kandhro said.Kandhro said 21% of young women in Sindh had been married before turning 18. She also flagged concerns around teenage pregnancies and limited access to maternal healthcare.According to her, Pakistan sees an estimated 61,000 pregnancies among girls aged 15 to 19 each year. Only 44% of pregnant girls in this age group receive at least four antenatal visits, she said.Kandhro also cited anaemia among girls in Sindh, putting the figure at 61.9%. She described this as the highest rate among the provinces.The speakers urged stronger safeguards for women and children and called for greater international attention to child and forced marriage, which they linked to gender-based violence.
Article Summary: UN rights event highlights risks faced by girls in Pakistan’s child marriages. Women's rights activist Shagufta Kandhro highlighted the situation of girls who are married before reaching adulthood. She also flagged concerns around teenage pregnancies and limited access to maternal healthcare.

Article Title: Motorcycle-borne gunmen kill 3 cops in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa
Article Text:
TTP suspicion after 3 traffic cops killed in Pakistan gun attack (ANI file photo)

Three traffic police officers were killed and three others injured in a gun attack in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Monday, the Associated Press cited police.The attack took place in Wazirabad Bazaar in Tank district when suspected militants on motorcycles opened fire on a vehicle carrying the traffic police.The attackers fled the area after the shooting, local police official Jamshed Khan said.No group has claimed responsibility for the latest attack. Police are likely to suspect the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which has carried out several attacks in the region. The TTP is a separate group from Afghanistan’s Taliban but is allied with it.The attack on police officials came two days after 'fidayeen' bomb blast in Dera Ismail Khan city in the same province. The suicide bombing killed at least 13 people and wounded over 30 others.Gunmen also opened fire on an ambulance that arrived at the scene. The TTP claimed responsibility for that attack.Pakistan has repeatedly accused Afghanistan’s Taliban government of allowing TTP militants to operate from Afghan territory and carry out attacks in Pakistan.Kabul has denied the allegations and said it does not allow its territory to be used against other countries.
Article Summary: Three traffic police officers were killed and three others injured in a gun attack in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Monday. Police are likely to suspect the Tehrik-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which has carried out several attacks in the region. The TTP is a separate group from Afghanistan’s Taliban but is allied with it.

Article Title: 20-year-old Azerbaijani woman allegedly drugged, gang-raped in Pakistan's Lahore
Article Text:
Azerbaijani woman, 20, allegedly drugged and gang-raped in Lahore; 3 booked (AP file photo)

A 20-year-old woman from Azerbaijan was allegedly gang-raped by three men in Lahore after being taken to a flat in the Defence Housing Authority area, news agency PTI cited police on Sunday.The incident allegedly took place after the woman, who came to Pakistan from Baku for business, was taken to a cafe by two women late on September 25. Police said three men joined them at the cafe around 11 pm and later offered to drop them in their vehicle.Instead, the men allegedly took the Azerbaijani woman to a flat, where they gave her an intoxicating substance and sexually assaulted her, according to police.She was later left near Lahore's Ghazi Interchange. The suspects allegedly took her iPhone before abandoning her.Police officer Anjum Bashir said the woman had been staying in Lahore's Raiwind area since arriving in Pakistan more than two weeks ago.Police have registered a case against three men and identified the main accused. Raids are being conducted to arrest the suspects, while their names have also been placed on the stop list to prevent them from leaving the country.The vehicle allegedly used in the incident has been recovered from the house of a relative of the main accused, Bashir said.Investigators are also examining the role of the two women who allegedly took the victim to the cafe.The woman has undergone a medical examination and police have registered the case under relevant provisions of the Pakistan Penal Code.
Article Summary: Azerbaijani woman, 20, allegedly drugged and gang-raped in Lahore; 3 booked. Incident allegedly took place after the woman was taken to a cafe by two women. Police said three men joined them at the cafe and later offered to drop them in their vehicle.

Article Title: 'Tarique hasn't ruled out India visit': Dhaka
Article Text:
Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman

DHAKA: PM Tarique Rahman has "not ruled out" a visit to India through a proper bilateral framework, Dhaka said Monday, stressing New Delhi must prevent individuals based in India from using its territory to make political statements or engage in activities aimed at destabilising Bangladesh."Restraining an extremist in their land is not too much to ask," state minister for foreign affairs Humaiun Kobir said, a reference to a past news conference of former Bangladesh PM Sheikh Hasina. Bangladesh would not allow anyone from India to use Bangladeshi territory to make statements against India, he told reporters."To maintain relations with another country, bilateral engagement is required. We will do it directly. The (PM's) visit will be bilateral, and we will talk," he said. "We must address the challenge of trust. Without trust, partnerships weaken," Kobir said.
Article Summary: Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman has "not ruled out" a visit to India through a proper bilateral framework. Rahman stresses New Delhi must prevent individuals based in India from using its territory to make political statements or engage in activities aimed at destabilising Bangladesh.

Article Title: Nepal ends flood search with over 5,000 still missing, including 189 Indians

Article Title: India's political will needed to extradite Sheikh Hasina: Bangladesh
Article Text:
File photo: Former Bangladesh PM Sheikh Hasina

DHAKA: Bangladesh on Sunday hoped India would act on its request for former PM Sheikh Hasina's extradition and expedite the process, saying that "while legal process is certainly a factor, political will is also essential".The remarks came a day after Indian high commissioner to Dhaka Dinesh Trivedi at the Bay of Bengal Conversation made it clear the legal process concerning extradition is ongoing and no time-frame can be given as courts are involved. He had said that "again and again, Indian govt has replied to this that there is a process, and the process is legal, and it is well structured. So, as far as that is concerned, the process is on"."While the legal process is certainly a factor, political will is also essential. We hope govt of India will focus on expediting the ongoing extradition process to bring the accused back. Both countries must possess political will. We certainly have political will, and they (India) need to have it as well," state minister for foreign affairs Shama Obaed Islam told reporterswhen asked about Trivedi's remarks.Meanwhile, outgoing Bangladesh high commissioner to India Md Riaz Hamidullah Sunday met Indian external affairs minister Dr S Jaishankar in New Delhi and discussed issues of mutual interest.During his 18-month stint in India as high commissioner, Riaz said he tried to quietly advance Bangladesh-India relations, premised on mutual trust, dignity and shared benefits.
Article Summary: Bangladesh on Sunday hoped India would act on its request for former PM Sheikh Hasina's extradition. Indian high commissioner to Dhaka Dinesh Trivedi made it clear the legal process concerning extradition is ongoing and no time-frame can be given as courts are involved.
